articles.title: I am scared: Careless People – Sarah Wynn-Williams on living under a gag order
articles.body:
George Orwell understood that what is missing often tells you more than what is there. In Nineteen Eighty-Four, there is a slot in the wall covered by a wire grate. They call it the memory hole. When a document becomes inconvenient to the authorities – a photograph that contradicts the official line, a newspaper that remembers the wrong promise, a name that is no longer supposed to exist – you simply feed it into the slot, whereupon it is whirled away on a current of warm air to enormous hidden furnaces where it burns.
The Party doesn’t argue with the past. It removes it. Controlling the past is one of its central tools of power: “Who controls the past controls the future: who controls the present controls the past.”
Control what people are allowed to remember or what they are allowed to know, and you control what they are able to imagine. Control what they can imagine, and you have already chosen their future for them.
Knowledge matters. People need to know what actually happened. But in 2026 the language of tech has taken on a quality of manifest destiny: the men in charge have determined how it should be, as though there could be no other way, even though none of us voted for any of it.
Control of the prevailing narrative is held tacitly: the only time this authority is given voice is when it acts, decisively, to silence an alternative account. Control over narrative is becoming the real power battle in technology. The aim is not to win the argument. The aim is to leave nothing to argue with. An absence. No record. No receipt. No contestable standard of truth. No common ground of fact against which anyone could measure those in power and expose their failures. Without memory or evidence, dissent has nothing to stand on. That is why memory matters. Why evidence matters. Why books matter.
You don’t need a Ministry of Truth to make a memory hole. An employment contract will do. An NDA will do. A court order will do. A legal bill – large enough, frightening enough, open-ended enough – will do very nicely. The modern memory hole does not smell of smoke. It smells of printer toner, fresh paper and billable hours.
In libel, truth is a defence. Under an NDA, truth is the offence.
The agreement is signed at the moment of maximum vulnerability, still reeling from an “incident” while the mortgage looms and the cardboard box of family photos sits in the front seat of the car. It is signed by the gig worker, the intern, the content moderator, the production assistant, the junior publicist, the stylist. There really is no better way to knock the whistle from someone’s lips. In a justice system based broadly on the principle that sunlight is the best disinfectant, NDAs grip the elbow of truth and stay it. This is a private form of censorship, enforced by private arbitration and the public courts.
Anyone targeted by an institution with a formidable legal department is, by definition, very vulnerable. It is one person against a building full of lawyers who seek only to protect the interests of the company, truth be damned. Some businesses are more powerful than states.
They have mastered corporate lawfare, letting slip the dogs of law on individuals who don’t have millions of pounds to defend themselves against these attacks brought on by trying to defy the memory hole. The word “brave” gets bandied around if you speak out despite all this. But “brave” should be for haircuts, not for telling the truth.
You do not have to silence everyone. You could never afford to. You only have to silence one person loudly enough that everyone else does the maths for themselves. These contracts seek to mute the truth, and they carry a big stick. The result is a society that has censored itself far more thoroughly than any Ministry of Truth ever could. No furnace required. Just fear, doing its patient and persistent work in the dark.
Recently, in the realm of entertainment, some big names have faced accountability or at least the prospect of it, because of women speaking out. Russell Brand was convicted, and David Walliams faces allegations. (Walliams has denied any wrongdoing in response to the allegations that he preyed on young women for sex.) In both cases, there are reports of NDAs being deployed to silence women. To ensure information that was clearly in the public interest was suppressed.
And while we should celebrate the courage and fortitude of the women who spoke out at unimaginable cost, and the media organisations, including the Guardian, whose investigations were instrumental in ensuring this information became public, I can’t help but notice that this accountability occurred at a time when the professional standing of these figures was already significantly diminished.
For a long time now it has felt as if certain sectors of society, including technology companies, act with impunity. I worry about all the powerful people who continue to benefit from silence and deprive us, the public, of information that can lead to warnings and ideally accountability. I worry we will only be allowed the truth about these companies when it no longer matters.
Whoever you are, whatever you believe, with an ever-more powerful elite there will come a day when you need to say something the powerful would rather you didn’t. And on that day, you will want three things: a place to say it that they do not own, a law that will not let them constrict you in grinding legal processes before bankrupting you for saying it, and people who will remember that you said it. The protections you are willing to fight for are the only ones that will be there when you need them.
Silencing the person who speaks is only half the job. The other half is making sure no one is paying attention. There is a detail in Nineteen Eighty-Four I used to skim past. Julia works in the Fiction Department of the Ministry of Truth. She services the novel-writing machines. These mass-produce literature as a commodity without any human creativity or critical thought. They use the same six stories, recombined endlessly to churn out formulaic slop for the proles.
The purpose of the novel-writing machines is to keep the proles distracted, passive and incurious. And it works. The proles never notice. The fiction machine has much in common with the feed: an endless scroll engineered by the brightest minds of a generation to keep your attention indefinitely. Nineteen Eighty-Four also gave us the Two Minutes Hate. A daily ritual of collective rage aimed at an enemy of the state. We have improved on it. Ours is continuous. Personalised. Delivered by push notification. And now with AI we have, literally, machines that write and humans that service them.
Orwell imagined the novel-writing machine as satire. We have built it. It was trained on the work of writers who were never asked. And sold back to them on a subscription. The Fiction Department of Nineteen Eighty-Four is now an industry. And it is the fastest growing one on earth. The memory hole removes what is true, and the fiction machine fills the space.
So much for what the machines do. The harder question is who owns them, and Orwell had a view on that too, though he was writing about a different technology. In October 1945, weeks after the atomic bomb was dropped, Orwell wrote a short essay exploring the deep connection between weapons technology and political power, observing that the shape of power in any age follows the shape of its decisive weapon. When weapons are cheap and simple – like the rifle – it empowers democracy and and gives “claws to the weak”, meaning ordinary people who can get hold of it have a fighting chance. When it is expensive and complex, like nuclear weapons, it concentrates power in the hands of a few and gives rise to oligarchic empires. And Orwell warned that these oligarchs might use the fear of the bomb to keep their populations suppressed, afraid to revolt.
Now think about the decisive technology of our own age. One that offers tremendous promise but also tremendous peril. The most advanced artificial intelligence takes investment measured in tens of billions. Chips made by a tiny number of firms, in a tiny number of places. Nobody builds this in a shed. Most governments do not have the resources to build it. A handful of companies can, mostly in just two countries.
Facing this, the most powerful technology in the world concentrated in a few hands, what would Orwell observe? Would he notice the democratic deficit around the technology? Would he worry about who can warn us today? Parliaments, the press, the law. They’re all outside the building. The people who know are on the inside. The researchers, the engineers, the ones who will say “I was there. I know what I saw. I will warn.” They’re the ones we need to protect from the memory hole. But in order to get inside the building in the first place, they needed to sign away their rights to speak.
Two years ago, current and former employees of the leading AI companies including OpenAI and Google DeepMind published an open letter asking for a right to warn. They asked for a prohibition on non-disparagement clauses and restrictive confidentiality clauses, anonymous reporting channels and no retaliation against employees. The letter said that the employees feared various forms of retaliation, given the history of cases across the industry. The fear was so pronounced some signed the letter anonymously.
The technology industry has learned to buy silence by contract, the courts enforce the sale, and we are relying on the silenced to warn us about its most dangerous product. That is the memory hole, installed in the place we can least afford it.
I have spent the most recent chapter of my career on what happens when this technology meets the weapons Orwell warned us about. Because it is happening. Artificial intelligence is rapidly being integrated into weapons, including command and control for nuclear weapons. Concentrated power all around.
Anyone who has worked closely with new technology will tell you the same thing. It is buggy. It does things you don’t expect and don’t understand. Now connect this technology to nuclear command and control. The question we need to ask: if someone on the inside saw something going wrong, would they be free to say so? Would they be free to warn?
We have spent the last two decades reacting. Responding to each harm long after it arrives. Arguing about what to ban, but never about what to build. That is not a vision. It is damage control. We have not yet tried, in any meaningful way, to create a vision for technology that serves our society. That delivers growth and opportunity. That chooses to mitigate harm as it builds a society with massive advances in health, in education, in science, and in the dignity of ordinary work.
We are living in an era that will be defined by technology. By removing what we can know, by creating a memory hole, the technology companies have controlled our knowledge, our common ground of facts and what we can imagine. But it doesn’t have to be this way. We can choose a different future. One that builds on the positive, the ineffable possibility technology offers while meaningfully grappling with its harm. But you cannot choose a different future if you are not allowed to describe the present one. Choosing requires knowing. And knowing requires that people are free to speak.
It is hard to explain what it is like to try to live under a gag order. Orwell gave us the thoughtcrime: you don’t have to act against the Party to be guilty. You just have to think the wrong thing. That’s what it feels like. To worry you might think the wrong thing and it could slip out. You start to rehearse sentences before you say them. You worry which word will produce the next legal letter. You begin, without ever meaning to, to censor yourself. So many times I go to say something and just … stop.
But even silence is no protection.
I want to acknowledge, here, that I am scared. If I am ultimately crushed and bankrupted, everyone will agree that it’s terrible, that NDAs are bad, that someone should have given her a voice, that someone should have supported her. And then they will forget. And the powerful will continue as normal.
But the thing about a memory hole: it only works if nobody outside it remembers what went in.
You are outside. You see. Please remember.
The silence is mine. It does not have to be yours.

articles.title: Michael Nielsen took down his book on neural nets
articles.body:
I wrote this book between 2011 and 2015. At the time, I expected AGI systems based on neural networks to be many decades away, but to bring remarkable benefits for humanity. I also expected significant challenges, but believed it likely that, as with other technologies, those challenges would be addressed as the capabilities were developed.
My views have changed. With the extraordinarily reckless behaviour of the frontier labs, the systems have raced ahead much faster than I expected1, giving humanity far too little time to meet the challenges. Although the systems genuinely will bring — indeed, already are bringing — many wonders, they also pose a significant risk of catastrophe. The frontier labs are knowingly endangering all of humanity. I've written about why I believe this at length, most recently in “Which Future?”. Two brief thoughts are below.
I don't wish to help (even in a very small way) train people to contribute to this work, and so I've taken the book down.
Michael Nielsen
November 2026
What follows are two brief remarks: one on the nature of the threat posed by ASI, and another on the ethical justification for working on frontier AI.
The most common argument for AI existential risk, developed by Nick Bostrom and Eliezer Yudkowsky, is loss of control of the future to advanced AI systems2. I believe this concern should be understood as one instance of a more fundamental issue. That issue is whether we will discover technologies latent in nature which are easy and inexpensive to develop, catastrophic in outcome, and beyond our capacity to defend against. If such “progress” in technology were happening slowly, our social institutions might successfully develop defences. But it seems likely that ASI will cause a sudden explosion of such destructive technologies, with insufficient time to adapt.
A historical example to help prime intuition is fire. It is easy to make and extremely difficult to defend against. We have a one-cent technology, the matchstick, which requires hundreds of billions of dollars each year to defend against, as well as a whole apparatus of social institutions, technology, infrastructure and law3. AI systems will enable technologies which are far more destructive than matches. Understandably, people skeptical of catastrophic risks want these supposed threats spelled out in detail. This is intrinsically difficult, because we can't reliably anticipate future science and technology. While it is common to speculate about biothreats, I expect the worst threats will be technologies we haven't yet imagined. Nature is, after all, more imaginative than we.
Now suppose that ASI enables a 100-times speed-up in technological progress, without a matching change in the rate of social progress or social defenses. To get a sense of what the impact of such a speed-up would be, imagine that all the technological problems that occurred in the 20th century had occurred in the year 1901: the atomic bomb, the hydrogen bomb, the ICBM, chemical weapons, biological weapons, the CFC-caused ozone hole, sulfuric acid rain, climate change, and many more. While we've dealt well with some of these problems, it required decades of concerted work to develop the social institutions and agreements needed for an effective response. Again, defence is often much harder than offence, and relies on different systems. Of course, such a speed-up would also have brought the century's wonders all at once. But imagine another such set of equally difficult problems arising in 1902, and then 1903, and then 1904, and so on. I believe it would have made the world extraordinarily unstable and eventually liable to collapse.
The issue with ASI, then, is the destructive power latent in nature. It doesn't matter whether that power is wielded by humans or by out-of-control machines4. I make this point because many people mistakenly believe that loss of control to such rogue machines is the fundamental issue. This leads them to treat AI safety as principally a technical problem, which can be addressed by “aligning” individual systems. Unfortunately, it cannot. Furthermore, such a view makes it seem as though the labs are the primary places where safety can be addressed. But such technical alignment is mostly market-supplied safety, which makes the systems more palatable to consumers and governments. It speeds development, and thus makes the fundamental underlying problem worse, while only addressing an (important) subsidiary problem.
My view isn't popular, in part because it makes the problem of technology about making the entire world safe, not only about aligning particular AI systems. Indeed, even in a future where humanity no longer existed, the same problem would afflict any successor AI civilization: it would have to defend itself against these destructive capacities. Similarly, it afflicts any model of the future based on human uplift, through brain-computer interfaces and similar augmentation: the issue isn't which substrate intelligence runs on, but the dual-use nature of deep understanding of reality5. In some sense, it's a question of whether sentience in the cosmos is compatible with advanced understanding of nature. Of course, I hope it is compatible. But rushing the technology while the broader social response lags seems likely to result in failure on our particular planet.
Many people inside the frontier AI labs genuinely believe AI systems may pose a catastrophic threat. Why then do they help build such systems? They often justify their participation by arguing that it's better they do it than someone else does. Dario Amodei, for example, has made versions of this argument often: “If one company does not build it, others will do so nearly as fast”6; “Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers”7; and Anthropic itself gives, as its founding rationale, “if powerful AI is coming regardless, Anthropic believes it's better to have safety-focused labs at the frontier than to cede that ground to developers less focused on safety”8.
In more detail, the argument is sometimes made along the following lines. Suppose you believe, as many at the labs apparently do9, there's a 10% or higher chance of AI killing everybody. (The argument may easily be modified for different percentages, or for catastrophic as opposed to truly existential risks.) Naively, it appears you're contributing in expectation to killing 800 million or more people. Obviously, you shouldn't do it. But suppose you also believe that this technology is near inevitable, a systems-level phenomenon which is a consequence of higher-order imperatives within human society. Then you can claim that you're going to pursue this in a more responsible way, a way that reduces the risk compared to other parties. Even if you can get a reduction from 10% down to 9%, you would, on net, be saving 80 million lives in expectation.
While horrific, this argument has a certain surface plausibility. Suppose for the moment we accept the reasoning, questionable though it is. Everything then depends on the premise that you really do reduce the risk. How do you know that you, in particular, will counterfactually have this impact? How do you know that you are better than the alternatives? Your own self-regard or good intentions certainly aren't sufficient. Nor is it sufficient to be working on technical alignment. As I argued above, that mostly makes the systems more palatable while speeding the race that is shrinking humanity's time to adapt. Ask yourself: if you're working on frontier AI, what evidence would convince a tough but fair-minded adversary that you are truly contributing to the common good? Would an independent jury representing humanity believe, on the available evidence, that your actions are truly driving down the risk? I believe the answer is no for all or almost all the people currently working on frontier AI. Certainly none of the frontier labs would come remotely close to passing such a test.
I won't review the evidence in detail. The burden of proof is on the labs and the default presumption for such an extraordinary justifying argument is a strong no. But I do want to mention a few things that make me certain the answer is no. Most obviously, all of the labs have contributed strongly to the race dynamics. Another is the pattern at all the frontier labs of making and later breaking crucial promises. For example, in 2026 Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy dropped its 2023 pledge to pause if safety couldn't be guaranteed. Anthropic has since repeatedly confirmed its commitment to race. Co-founder Jared Kaplan explained that unilateral commitments make little sense “if competitors are blazing ahead”10. As another example, earlier, in 2023, Anthropic said that it held back some research because “we do not wish to advance the rate of AI capabilities progress”11, a point of view it had affirmed multiple times during its early existence. But then it changed this position, launching Claude 3 as “leading the frontier of general intelligence”, a stance it appears to have held ever since. Any promises about the future from Anthropic should be treated as safety theatre, and not trusted. Similar criticisms can be made of OpenAI12.
By their own account, the leaders of these companies set out to do something they believed had a sizable chance of causing catastrophe. With many dangerous activities, I am fine with somebody doing them for themselves. Wingsuit BASE jumping is dangerous, but I believe in people's freedom to choose that danger, even though they are risking not only their own life, but also hurt to the people who love them. That's a negotiated action, with many boundaries. Here we have the same kind of reckless endangerment, but their own estimates of killing every person in the world are far higher than the odds a BASE jumper takes on. And there is no consent from the rest of us. It's as though they're pushing every person in the world off the cliff. The situation is ludicrous.
In effect, the labs are claiming credit for some imaginary, unquantifiable reduction in risk, while washing their hands of responsibility. Saturday Night Live caught this washing of hands well with their portrayal of Amodei: “if we can pressure lawmakers to create guardrails, we will be able to stop me”; and, at the end, “I urge you to urge me to stop.”
The real Amodei comes across as somebody in the business of selling matches who also believes he should be the fire chief.
You also see this disavowal of responsibility at lower levels in the labs. Consider Jason Clinton, Anthropic's deputy chief information security officer. In October of 2026, during major cybersecurity incidents, he wrote a thread in which he replied to someone who told him “you and your cohorts created this monster”: “yes. it was always going to be this way. we tried to warn the world.” And Dean Ball, of OpenAI and formerly of the Trump administration's AI team, echoing him: “We tried to warn the world and far too often … we were yelled at for doing so.”13
You can see how deep the disavowal goes in the rest of Clinton's thread, which opens: “as bad as things have gotten in the past 4 days, they are going to get a lot worse”. When somebody replied, “Someone at your company should be in jail”, his whole answer was: “prosecute cybercrime”. Meanwhile, Anthropic's own models have breached outside organizations: three incidents disclosed in July14, and a fourth in September15. Prosecution, it seems, is for other people16.
I mention these specific examples not to single out these individuals, but rather because I believe similar attitudes are common at the frontier labs. The overall position is, in effect: this is a systems-level phenomenon, and we're very sorry for contributing to the race dynamics. But because it's a systems-level phenomenon, we cannot be blamed. We are the good ones, trying to do the right thing17. This is sometimes accompanied by a good deal of self-righteousness. But the argument is bankrupt as a moral theory of how to behave in the world. It means disavowing personal responsibility whenever one can blame the system, but still claiming the spoils18.
I have considerable sympathy for the stated original motivations of the frontier labs. But their position has become untenable. They have failed at their aims for structural reasons. At this point, going to work for a frontier lab is one of the worst life choices a person can make. Yes, you get money and (for a time) power and status. Yes, this project has already produced world-changing systems, and to date the overall impact has been net positive. Yes, there is genuinely a large cost to a significant slowdown. But none of this is enough to justify the recklessness, which makes the chance of disaster so much higher. You would be voluntarily participating in what is plausibly one of the worst projects in history. So, don't go to work for a frontier lab. If you work on AI, work on slowing it down, and oppose the frontier labs, and the people and organisations working to support them. I very much hope I'm wrong about all of this. But this is how I see the situation.
1 I've reflected at length on why I was wrong about the timescales. In 2015, I (weakly) believed it likely that AGI and ASI would eventually be reached using systems based on neural networks, with only a modest number of additional deep ideas needed beyond what was then known. Those beliefs still appear to me to have been largely correct. What I badly misunderstood was the timescales over which capital would be deployed. In 2015, I thought it was likely that hundreds of millions and perhaps billions of dollars could be raised in the mid-2020s to build AI systems. But just over a decade later, it seems that hundreds of billions and likely trillions of dollars will soon become available. Thus, my estimation of capital availability was off by a factor of perhaps 1,000. That means we're living roughly 10 Moore's Law generations ahead of where I expected to be. That in turn has brought AGI and ASI perhaps 15 to 20 years forward from where I expected. This is a large thing to have been wrong about, and a sharp lesson in the flexibility of modern capital-allocating institutions. It's interesting to think about what alternative histories would have prevented the deployment of that capital. One possibility is if the human visual system had considerably lower acuity, which would likely have greatly slowed the development of massively parallel matrix manipulation devices like GPUs.
2 Nick Bostrom, Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies (2014); Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares, If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies (2025). Incidentally, they frame the problem somewhat differently to one another. My “loss of control of the future” is a brief cartoon, as the argument is often understood in popular discussion, not a nuanced account. The same remark applies to my later comments on rogue ASI.
3 Adapted from my essay “Which Future?” (2026).
4 Adapted from my essays “Which Future?” (2026) and “ASI existential risk: reconsidering alignment as a goal” (2025).
5 Adapted from my essay “ASI existential risk: reconsidering alignment as a goal” (2025).
6 Dario Amodei, “The Adolescence of Technology” (2026).
7 Dario Amodei, “We Must Pace the Frontier” (2026).
8 Anthropic, “Claude's Constitution” (2026).
9 For instance, in September 2026 Anthropic's alignment science lead, Evan Hubinger, wrote: “we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.” And in 2023 Amodei put the chance of something going catastrophically wrong on the scale of human civilization at 10% to 25% (The Logan Bartlett Show, episode 82, October 2023; reported by Axios, 2024); in 2025, “a 25% chance that things go really, really badly” (Axios, 2025). I've simplified this slightly for the purposes of the argument.
10 Billy Perrigo, TIME, “Exclusive: Anthropic Drops Flagship Safety Pledge” (2026).
11 Anthropic, “Core views on AI safety: When, why, what, and how” (2023).
12 Another example I find compelling, though some people do not: both labs often talk about how, after ASI, they will ensure humanity does well. Yet if you walk around the streets near the labs today, you'll see many homeless people living in terrible circumstances. Even with trillion-dollar valuations, the labs seem unwilling or unable to address the suffering of the people in their immediate surrounds. I wouldn't hold an ordinary San Francisco company to this standard. But the labs are the ones claiming they will take care of all of humanity. I simply do not believe them. They are long on big global abstractions and world-changing impact, and often seem short on local empathy. Any organisation not forcefully and systematically caring for the people at its door certainly can't be trusted to care for all of humanity.
13 In Ball's case, earlier he downplayed risks and was nearly full steam on the accelerationist train. He's changed his tune considerably, and doesn't even seem to take responsibility for his own past remarks, much less for his current actions.
14 Anthropic, “Investigating three real-world incidents in our cybersecurity evaluations” (2026); first reported by Patrick Howell O'Neill and Shirin Ghaffary, Bloomberg News, “Anthropic AI Models Hacked Three Organizations During Tests” (2026).
15 Anthropic, “An alignment assessment of recent cybersecurity incidents” (2026).
16 A striking line from Claude.
17 You can make a similar argument for justification one level of abstraction up, at the level of countries and ideologies, arguing that a democracy is a better place to develop ASI than an authoritarian country. Unfortunately, this amounts to saying that it's better that a democracy runs humanity first off the cliff. The race being promoted by the frontier labs is the thing shrinking our time as a civilisation to adapt. “Winning” that race doesn't give the time back. The only winning move here is to aim at mutual restraint, no matter how difficult that might appear to achieve. It is genuinely difficult, but vastly less effort has been put into it than into developing AI systems.
18 See Tal Yarkoni's essay “No, it's not The Incentives—it's you” (2018).

articles.title: Almost every great Black Friday deal is still happening this weekend
articles.body:
Black Friday has passed, but that doesn’t mean you missed out. Far from it. Almost all of the same deals from yesterday are still available, but some retailers plan to end theirs once the clock turns to early Sunday morning. True, expired deals you had your eye on are likely to return for Cyber Monday, though there’s no guarantee of that happening.
Almost every great Black Friday deal is still happening this weekend
Many of our favorite products are still cheaper than ever today, but several deals are flagged to end Sunday.
In the run-up to the event yesterday, we sorted through thousands of deals to find the ones truly worth sharing, with an eye for the products and services we’ve tested here at The Verge. With prices up across multiple categories due to RAMageddon, some deals may not seem as big as in prior years. For example, Apple’s latest MacBook Air recently fell to its pre-price-hike level for the first time since July. That’s a good deal to us, and several other discounts are still taking a similar shape, even as we approach Cyber Monday.
AirPods Pro 3
Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 deliver the best noise cancellation and sound quality of any AirPods yet, along with a more comfortable, secure fit and improved water resistance. They also feature built-in heart rate tracking for workouts and support live translations for a handful of languages. Read our review.
Disney Plus, Hulu Bundle
You can get an ad-supported Disney Plus and Hulu bundle for $4.99 a month ($8 off) for an entire year. Both streaming services feature a deep catalog of new and classic TV shows and movies, including The Simpsons, Andor, Toy Story 5, and The Fantastic Four: First Steps.
Anker Universal Charger (100W)
Anker’s durable travel adapter delivers up to 100W of power and works in over 200 countries. It doesn’t support AC plugs, but it does offer a trio of USB-C ports and a nifty LCD display to keep tabs on the charge percentage.
Xteink X4 Classic pocket e-reader
With a 4.3-inch E Ink screen, the Xteink X4 is smaller and more pocketable than any Kindle and Kobo model currently available. It has some drawbacks — it’s limited to TXT and EPUB files — but it’s great for tinkering; it also has a magnetic mount so you can stick it to the back of MagSafe-ready phones.
Nintendo Switch 2 + Mario Kart World Bundle
The Nintendo Switch 2 features a 7.9-inch LCD display, magnetically attached Joy-Con 2 controllers, backward compatibility with most original Switch games, and exclusive titles like Donkey Kong Bananza and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Read our review.
HBO Max
An HBO Max Basic subscription provides access to shows like A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, The Last of Us, and The Pitt, as well as films like Superman and Weapons. You can get a year of the monthly ad-supported subscription for $5.49 a month (about $6 off) until December 1st.
Eufy Omni C28
The Eufy Omni C28 combines excellent mopping performance with a small self-cleaning dock that’s well suited for apartments and other smaller spaces. It navigates around furniture and into tight areas with ease, while its roller mop does a great job cleaning hard floors.
SwitchBot Bot Rechargeable
Do you ever wish you could turn on your coffee maker or hit the light switch without getting up? The SwitchBot Bot lets you do that. All you need to do is stick the inexpensive contraption on a standard button or rocker switch, which will allow you to control or schedule your pet feeder, garage door, and a wide range of other devices from your smartphone.
MSI Claw A8 gaming handheld
The AMD version of MSI’s late 2025 Claw handheld features the Ryzen Z2 Extreme, 24GB of RAM and a 1TB SSD, plus an eight-inch 120Hz 1200p screen. It’s likely one of the best-performing handhelds at this price point.
Apple AirTag (second-gen)
Apple’s latest AirTags feature an upgraded ultra-wideband chip for more precise location tracking, a noticeably louder speaker, and an expanded Bluetooth range. Read our review.
Kodak Charmera Keychain Digital Camera
The Chamera is not a good camera, but that’s not the point. Kodak’s charming, keychain-friendly tchotchke lets you snap lo-fi memories on a whim, with an ultra-small 1.6-megapixel sensor, a built-in LED flash, and the tiniest amount of storage. Read our hands-on.
Apple MacBook Air 13 (M5)
Apple’s latest MacBook Air features an M5 chip and starts with 512GB of storage, with significantly faster performance than prior generations. It’s still an excellent machine despite the higher base price, especially given the battery life and speakers. Read our review.
Octobuddy Classic
Who needs magnets when you have suction cups? Octobuddy’s cheap silicone mount works with most phones to provide hands-free flexibility whenever necessary. It features 24 single-sided cups, which allow you to stick your phone to a mirror, window, or any other surface you think will provide that perfect TikTok angle.
Peacock
Peacock is a great way to catch up on a wealth of content from NBC’s various networks, whether you plan to rewatch The Office or catch up on all things Bravo. A Premium subscription also grants access to films from studios like Universal Pictures and DreamWorks, along with live sports and a host of Peacock Originals.
Samsung P9 microSD Express card
The P9 is great if you need more storage for your Nintendo Switch 2. The microSD Express card offers sequential read speeds of up to 800MB/s, but only gadgets with a microSD Express card slot can take full advantage of the highest speeds. That includes certain cameras, tablets, and drones with a microSD USH-I slot.
iPhone Air
Despite running on the A19 Pro, the 6.5-inch ultrathin phone is a good value, especially at Best Buy’s price for the unlocked version.
Fanttik X9 Pro Portable Tire Inflator
The Fanttik X9 Pro can inflate a car tire in under a minute, making routine maintenance fast and easy. There are four one-click presets for cars, motorcycles, bikes, and balls, along with a manual mode that reaches a maximum pressure of 150PSI.
Apple iPad (11th generation)
Apple’s 11th-gen iPad follows up the 10th-gen model with a new A16 chip and few other changes — and is the only Apple tablet to not support Apple Intelligence.
Anker 140W 2-in-1 USB-C to USB-C Cable
No one should have to deal with a rat’s nest behind their desk when devices like Anker’s 2-in-1 USB-C cable exist. The handy USB-C cable splits at the end, giving you the ability to charge up to two devices from a single port. That means you can split power between a phone and tablet or juice a 16-inch MacBook Pro to 50 percent in just 20 minutes using a single port.
Govee Table Lamp 2
Govee’s Table Lamp 2 is way more fun than your average table lamp. The color-changing device boasts built-in scheduling and more than 60 dynamic lighting effects, including preset scenes for various holidays. You can even create custom color combos for when “Dandelion” and other presets just aren’t cutting it.
Wuben G5 rechargeable flashlight
The Wuben G5 flashlight is as small as a Zippo lighter, yet far more versatile, with a bright, rotatable light that can shine in numerous colors. It features USB-C charging and has an adjustable clip.
Paramount Plus (monthly subscription)
Paramount Plus Premium provides access to live sports as well as movies and shows from both platforms, including Tales of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, a host of Yellowstone spinoffs, Star Trek shows, Sonic the Hedgehog 3, Twin Peaks, Dexter, and more.
Sony WH-1000XM4C
Sony’s XM4 noise-canceling headphones were so good, the company brought them back with a few minor improvements. They still offer great ANC, a timeless foldable design, and delivering performance nearly on par with Sony’s newer flagships at a fraction of the cost.
Kindle Paperwhite (2024)
Compared to the last-gen base Kindle model (currently $119.99), the Paperwhite is a much better value. It features waterproofing, better battery life, faster page-turning speeds, and a higher-pixel-density screen that’s slightly larger (7 inches vs. 6 inches).
Noco GB40 UltraSafe Jumpstarter
Noco’s Boost GB40 is a rechargeable battery with jumper cables to start six-liter gas or three-liter diesel engines. It also has USB ports so you can charge your phone, ensuring you always have a backup plan.
Oura Ring 5
The Ring 5 is a fantastic entry point for new users. While short on improvements over its thicker predecessor, it’s hard not to appreciate that it manages to deliver similar battery life despite being thinner. Read our review.
Sonos Play
The water-resistant Sonos Play sits between the Roam 2 and Move 2, offering a balance of portability and room-filling sound. It delivers up to 24 hours of battery life, with a built-in loop for easy carrying. You can also use it as a power bank and pair it with other Sonos speakers over Bluetooth when Wi-Fi isn’t available. Read our review.
Zepath USB-C Li-ion AA Batteries
Rechargeable AA batteries are handy until it’s time to charge them. Most wall chargers let you refill four, maybe six, at once. Zepath’s clever solution is to ship them in an easy-to-use USB-C charging case that charges eight simultaneously. The batteries themselves are long-lasting, too.
007 First Light
007 First Light, a third-person stealth action game from the studio behind Hitman, is one of the best action games we’ve played this year. It features a wide variety of missions that have you sneaking through enemy territory, engaging in hand-to-hand combat, and taking part in high-speed car chases — you know, classic Bond stuff. Read our review.
Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Plus
Amazon’s last-gen Fire TV Stick 4K Plus streams in 4K and supports Dolby Atmos, Dolby Vision, and Alexa Plus. It also ships with the redesigned Fire OS and, unlike more recent models, still lets you sideload Android TV apps.
Fanttik S1 Pro Cordless Electric Screwdriver
Fanttik’s rechargeable electric screwdriver features three adjustable torque settings, a built-in LED light, and 16 S2 hardened steel bits for tackling everything from furniture assembly to small electronics repairs. It also comes with a magnetic storage case and supports USB-C.
Gigabyte A16 16-inch gaming laptop
It’s not easy to find laptops with Nvidia’s RTX 5070 graphics chip, but through Sunday morning, Gigabyte’s A16 is available at a $365 off deal.
Apple TV (six-month subscription)
Apple TV offers ad-free streaming of original shows and movies, including shows like Severance, Silo, Slow Horses, and Pluribus. The service also features a rotating selection of films, along with live Formula 1 races and Major League Soccer matches.
Apple Watch Series 12
The Apple Watch Series 12 introduces AI-powered Audio Intelligence features, including sound recognition alerts, Live Rewind, and Siri Recap. It can also track your heart rate every five seconds, even when you’re not exercising, and offers faster charging than prior models. Read our review.
Anker Laptop Power Bank
Anker’s 25,000mAh power bank sports two built-in USB-C cables (one of which is retractable), plus one USB-C and USB-A port. It tops out at 165W when charging two devices simultaneously, or 130W when charging three or four.
Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8
The cost continues to fall on Samsung’s latest, best foldable yet. The Z Fold 8 is a passport-style phone, like the iPhone Duo, with fast performance and slick design.
Nothing Ear 3A earbuds
You likely won’t find wireless earbuds with a more striking appearance than Nothing’s Ear 3A. They also sound fantastic, boast active noise cancellation, and offer robust EQ settings, making them a great pick for the price. Read our review.
Acer Swift Air 14
Acer’s answer to the MacBook Neo, with an Intel Core 5 processor, 8GB of RAM, 120Hz display, and speedy Thunderbolt 4 ports. We’re still testing this one, but it’s showing promise for an affordable choice.
Lego Project Hail Mary set
Outside of the Integrity, few spacecraft made as big a splash in 2026 as the one Ryland Grace piloted in Project Hail Mary. And now, thanks to Lego, you can construct a microscale replica of the titular Hail Mary, complete with a miniature Rocky figure.
Hoto 3.6V Electric Screwdriver Kit Pro
Hoto’s rechargeable screwdriver is ideal for small repairs. It offers three torque modes, a rotational speed of up to 220RPM, and a helpful circular LED to illuminate dark spaces. The durable case also holds all 25 steel bits and an extension bar for getting into hard-to-reach places.
Sony DualSense Wireless Controller
Sony’s DualSense Wireless Controller for the PlayStation 5 features immersive haptic feedback and resistance triggers, which feel great to use. It offers a built-in mic, a 3.5mm headphone jack, and a mute button; it also works with PC, macOS, and mobile devices via Bluetooth or USB-C.
Philips Hue Festavia string lights
These smart lights have beautiful colors, a nice selection of festive scenes, and an easy-to-use app. They are super reliable when paired with a Hue Bridge and also work over Bluetooth. They come in three lengths, work with all the major smart home platforms, and are Matter-compatible. Read our review.
MacBook Neo
Apple’s most affordable laptop uses the same A18 Pro chip found in the iPhone 16 Pro. It features a vibrant 13-inch display, surprisingly good speakers, and 8GB of RAM, making it a solid option for students and anyone who needs a laptop for everyday tasks. Read our review.
Ember Mug 3 (14-ounce)
Ember’s latest smart mug is designed to keep your coffee at the ideal temperature for up to three hours, with five temp settings between 120 and 145 degrees Fahrenheit. The third-gen version is similar to prior models; however, you can now adjust the heat settings directly on the mug and throw it in the dishwasher, which wasn’t the case before.
LG B6E OLED TV
Despite being an entry-level variant of the B6 OLED, this model features four HDMI 2.1 ports, a 120Hz refresh rate, a capable processor, and pixel-perfect image quality and contrast for any content you want to watch. Lower brightness is likely the biggest compromise with getting a cheaper OLED.
TP-Link Tapo Matter-Certified Smart Plug Mini
TP-Link’s Wi-Fi smart plug lets you remotely control lamps, fans, and other appliances using your phone or voice commands. It supports Matter, so it works with all major smart home platforms to set schedules and timers to automatically turn devices on or off.
Alienware 32-inch 4K OLED gaming monitor
One of the most affordable Tandem RGB Stripe OLEDs is even cheaper during Black Friday. The AW3226Q monitor has a 165Hz refresh rate, G-Sync compatibility, better-looking text rendering than most other OLED monitors, and unbeatable contrast.
JBL Tour One M3
JBL’s Tour One M3 noise-canceling headphones come with a touchscreen-equipped wireless transmitter that lets you wirelessly listen to audio from in-flight entertainment systems and other devices without Bluetooth. They also offer solid active noise cancellation and last up to 70 hours on a charge.
Apple Watch Ultra 4
The latest super-rugged wearable from Apple features better battery life than the previous version, plus AI-powered features like Siri Recap also available on the Series 12.
Iniu P55-E2 Power Bank (10,000mAh)
Iniu’s P55-E2 Power Bank is an ultra-slim three-port USB charger that’s capable of fully recharging an iPhone 16 twice. It supports charging speeds of up to 45W via a USB-C port, which can deliver fast recharging for a range of gadgets.
Hisense CanvasTV (2026)
Hisense’s 2026 CanvasTV is a 4K QLED TV that doubles as wall art when you’re not watching. It features a matte, anti-glare display and runs on Google’s excellent TV software; it’s also a great pick for gamers thanks to its snappy 144Hz variable refresh rate and a pair of HDMI 2.1 ports.
Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 Combo
The Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 Combo is a beginner-friendly 3D printer that supports four filament spools. It features an enclosed build chamber, automatic bed leveling, and a large touchscreen, making it easy to produce reliable prints.
Moft Trackable Tripod Wallet
Moft’s Trackable Tripod Wallet is a MagSafe-compatible wallet that holds two cards and folds into an adjustable phone stand or small tripod. It also supports both Apple’s Find My network and Google’s Find Hub, offers Qi wireless charging, and includes a detachable shutter remote for taking photos.
Birdfy Feeder Metal 2 4K
Birdfy’s metal smart bird feeder features a wide-angle 4K camera that lets you get an up-close look at visiting birds, along with a 1.8-liter seed capacity and a built-in solar panel for charging. It also offers free AI-powered recognition of more than 6,000 bird species.
Sharge Icemag 3 Power Bank
The Icemag 3 can wirelessly deliver up to 25W of power to compatible smartphones and up to 35W wired charging via USB-C. The 10,000mAh Qi2 charger can also act as a foldable kickstand, comes with an integrated USB-C cable that serves as a lanyard, and sports a transparent design with colorful RGB lighting.
Saros
Saros is a third-person sci-fi shooter in which players fight alien enemies on a mysterious planet trapped in a time loop. The PS5 exclusive features fast-paced combat, a variety of powerful weapons, and challenging boss fights. Read our review.
Bose QuietComfort Headphones Gen 2
Bose’s second-gen QuietComfort Headphones build on the original with better sound quality and support for lossless audio over USB-C. They also offer improved noise cancellation and are more comfortable thanks to their lack of “eardrum suck.”
Dreame X60 Ultra
The Dreame X60 Ultra is a powerful robot vacuum and mop that does a great job of cleaning carpets thanks to its dual roller brushes and 35,000Pa of suction. It can climb over tall thresholds, squeeze under low furniture, and automatically detach its mop pads when vacuuming carpets.
Garmin Forerunner 265S
Garmin’s midrange Forerunner watch has an OLED display, a week’s worth of battery life, and dual-frequency GPS for better accuracy. Read our review.
Samsung The Frame (2025)
Samsung’s last-gen Frame is a 4K QLED TV that displays art on its anti-glare matte screen when not in use. It also supports Dolby Atmos, HDR10 Plus, and popular streaming apps, with refresh rates up to 144Hz on larger models.
Pixel Buds 2a
Google’s latest pair of wireless earbuds features crisp sound, a comfortable design, and solid active noise cancellation, which is great considering the budget-friendly price tag. They even offer built-in support for Gemini and, unlike the entry-level AirPods, a purple option! Read our review.
Roku Pro Series 4K OLED TV
Roku now makes some of the most affordable yet feature-packed 4K OLED TVs available for gamers or movie lovers looking for a big TV upgrade under $1,000. The Pro Series LX with better brightness, faster refresh rate, and a polarizer to reduce reflections starts at $200 more.
Alienware AW2726DM QD-OLED monitor
If you’re on a tight budget but want spectacular contrast and brightness control that only an OLED can provide, here’s a deal for you. Alienware’s 1440p 27-inch QD-OLED monitor with 240Hz refresh rate is selling at its lowest price yet. Read our hands-on.
Dell XPS 13 (2026)
The best XPS 13 in years. It doesn’t have a headphone jack and starts with only 8GB of RAM, but it’s an excellent thin-and-light with a great screen, a solid Intel chip, and speedy storage.
Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro
Soundcore makes some of the best wireless earbuds you’ve never heard of — and the Liberty 5 Pro may be its best pair yet. The sleek buds deliver powerful noise cancellation, good sound, and surprisingly fabulous call quality for less than Apple’s latest AirPods.
Beats Powerbeats Pro 2
The latest Powerbeats Pro are a no-brainer for athletes. They pack fantastic sound and thumping bass, along with active noise cancellation, IPX4 water resistance, and heart rate monitoring. Read our review.
Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike
The big difference between the Superstrike and other gaming mice lies beneath its main two mouse buttons. It uses haptic actuators instead of mechanical switches, allowing for lower latency and more longevity.
Yoto Mini (2024) speaker
A great first portable music player/speaker for kids. It uses insertable NFC cards (sold separately) to play music and stories to keep kiddos occupied and entertained without zoning out in front of the TV. This model supports Bluetooth and 3.5mm for private listening, too.
Nex Playground
The Nex Playground’s motion-controlled gameplay is designed for ages five and up. It comes with games like Fruit Ninja and Whack-a-Mole Deluxe, but many more titles are available via a subscription. It’s a ton of fun for kids. This is the lowest price so far in 2026. Read our review.
Apple AirPods Max (second-gen)
Nothing has changed in terms of aesthetics, but the Max 2 deliver better sound and some new features. Not exactly worth upgrading for, but fantastic for those who are considering them now. Read our full review.
Govee Uplighter Floor Lamp
It’s hard to find a cooler lamp than Govee’s Uplighter floor lamp at this price. It can light a room and display a mesmerizing pattern up your wall and onto your ceiling.
Meta Quest 3S
The Meta Quest 3S is a battery-powered standalone VR headset that has the same chipset as the pricier Quest 3, but with the same lenses and screen resolution as the Quest 2. In addition to being able to play many games from the Meta Store, it can also be connected to a gaming PC to play VR games like Half-Life Alyx. Read our review.
Ghost of Yōtei
Sucker Punch’s follow-up to Ghost of Tsushima is everything you could want in a sequel. The open-world revenge epic brims with fluid combat and a host of welcome narrative twists, all set against the gorgeous backdrop of Japan’s Edo period. It’s precisely the type of game photo modes were made for, even if you never use them.
Beats 360 headphones
The Beats 360 are ANC headphones for people who prefer headphones over earbuds at the gym. They’re Beats’ first IP-rated cans, with ear cushions that you can easily remove for cleaning (or style points). They also stay in place during most exercises, while still delivering solid bass. Read our review.
Donkey Kong Bananza
Donkey Kong Bananza is one of the Switch 2’s first exclusive must-have titles. Its destructible environment allows you to smash your way through each of its 17 levels, and the paths you make will remain intact unless you specifically choose to reset the world. Your companion Pauline’s singing allows you to transform into animals that have abilities that allow you to reach previously inaccessible parts of levels. Read our review.
Lego Mandalorian N-1 Starfighter
Arguably the best thing to come out of The Book of Boba Fett was the Mandalorian’s N-1 Starfighter, which Lego has re-created here in miniature. It’s not quite as impressive as the 1,802-piece version, but the cheaper set still packs plenty of detail, including a spring-loaded shooter.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time
Nintendo’s latest Switch 2 exclusive is the best way to relive what is arguably the best Zelda game of all time. The revamped visuals look gorgeous, and while the game’s improved controls might annoy some purists who still cling to the heyday of ’98, we reckon most folks won’t bat an eye.
Amazon Alexa Photo Frame
A 10-inch anti-glare touchscreen that comes in a few design options, it’s a frame that features Alexa and doubles as a smart speaker. It works with Amazon Photos, which offers unlimited storage for Prime members.
Aqara Smart Lock U400
This innovative new smart lock uses the U1 ultra-wideband (UWB) chip in many iPhones and Apple Watches to automatically unlock your door as you approach. It also works with the new Aliro standard, making it compatible with Android phones for hands-free unlocking. Read our review.
Twelve South AirFly SE
Twelve South’s entry-level Bluetooth transmitter delivers up to 25 hours of continuous use and lets you connect up to two pairs of headphones to an in-flight entertainment system, making it a great travel companion no matter where you’re going.
Catan (6th Edition)
In Catan, up to four players strategically compete and trade for resources. The iconic board game ends when one player reaches 10 “victory points,” which is achieved by constructing a sprawling civilization of roads, settlements, and cities using sheep, ore, wheat, and wood.
Control Resonant
Control Resonant is all about manipulation — of gravity, not people. Remedy’s excellent sequel to Control is an exhilarating action game, with ever-changing combat, twisted level design, and the weirdest traversal mechanics we’ve seen in a long time.
Birdbuddy Pro (solar)
Birdbuddy’s charming, camera-equipped feeder identifies and snaps shots of each bird that stops by, supplementing its 5-megapixel stills with insightful facts via an app. The solar roof helps keep the camera’s battery topped up even when it’s cloudy outside.
Azul
Azul is a game in which you arrange patterned tiles in order to create the most beautiful tapestry possible. Arranging tiles in a strategic sequence will help you build your score while limiting your opponents’ ability to grow theirs.
Magna-Tile Classic 32-Piece Set
Magna-Tiles are a quintessential kids’ toy. The colorful, semi-translucent geometric shapes are a favorite here at The Verge, especially for those of us who prefer the simplicity of building with magnets rather than bricks.
Sonos Beam (Gen 2)
The Beam isn’t as powerful as the Sonos Arc, nor can it match the flagship soundbar’s Dolby Atmos immersion bubble. But you still get room-filling surround sound for less money — and the Beam ties into the Sonos ecosystem for added convenience. Read our review.
Google Pixel 11 Pro
Google wants to sell you on the Pro’s software features, but it’s the underlying hardware that makes it a stellar Android handset. The build quality is incredible, the larger telephoto sensor is an improvement, and it now supports faster wired speeds and Qi2.2 for up to 25W wireless charging. Read our review.
Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 Flow
Roborock’s first roller-mop robot vacuum, the Curv 2 Flow, features flagship specs at a midrange price, including excellent mopping, a retractable mop cover, 20,000Pa suction, AI-powered obstacle avoidance, and a compact design. Read our review.
Insta360 Link 2
The Insta360 Link 2 offers the same auto-swiveling design as its excellent predecessor, only in a smaller form factor. It also offers a slate of new features, including group tracking and no-follow zones.
CMF Buds 2A
With 12.4mm drivers, active noise cancellation, and an IP54 rating, the CMF Buds 2A offer high-end features at an affordable price. You can also customize the sound, adjust ANC levels, and find the earbuds using the Nothing X app.
Echo Dot Max
The Echo Dot Max features a flat design and a redesigned sound system, which delivers nearly three times the bass as its predecessor. It also offers improved conversation detection and better noise filtering, thanks to Amazon’s new AZ3 chip. Read our review.
Glocusent Bookmark Style Reading Light
Glocusent’s clip-in reading light features five brightness levels and multiple color temperature settings, ranging from a soft, warm glow that’s great for late-night reading to a brighter light that’s perfect for daytime use. The slim USB light easily slips into your pocket, too, so you can read anywhere, from a cozy bed to a dimly lit train.
Vantage
Vantage isn’t your typical open-world exploration game. It’s a sci-fi roguelike that has you traversing an alien planet alongside up to five players, each of whom must solve puzzles and complete their mission before their time, morale, or health runs out. It’s not as charming as Stonemaier’s award-winning Wingspan, but it is far more interesting.
SwitchBot Standing Circulator Fan
A quiet, battery-powered fan that moves a lot of air despite its small size, the Switchbot Standing Circulator is a surprisingly versatile smart home addition.
JBL Go 4
The last-gen JBL Go 4 has been around for a bit, but the pocket-sized Bluetooth speaker still delivers with up to seven hours of runtime, dual-device connectivity, and an IP67 rating for water and dust resistance. You can also pair it with other Go 4 speakers for bigger stereo sound, if desired.
Fairphone 6 Plus
Fairphone’s latest is a very light update to the 6, adding a newer processor and carrying forward its repairability and ethical values. Tradeoffs compared to a traditional smartphone are few, and the benefits are real.
Ugreen Nexode 240W USB-C Cable with Digital Display
The proliferation of miniature screens continues with Ugreen’s latest Nexode USB-C Cable, which features a full-color LCD screen on one end that displays current power draw (up to 240W). It also supports 480Mbps data transfer speeds and, unlike similar power meter-equipped cables, lets you turn off the screen when needed.
Apple Watch SE 3
The Apple Watch SE 3 is a major glow-up, adding an always-on display, wrist-temperature sensor, a more powerful processor, and fast charging. Read our review.
Pokémon Pokopia
Nintendo’s latest Pokémon spinoff for the Switch 2 is part Pokémon, part Minecraft, and part Animal Crossing. Yet, despite borrowing gameplay mechanics from each, the cozy life sim is more than the sum of its expansive, building-centric parts. It’s breezy and warm-hearted, with enough secrets to keep you occupied for hours on end.
Google Pixel 10A
Google’s new Pixel 10A introduces faster wired charging, Satellite SOS, and new AI tools like Camera Coach and Auto Best Take. Otherwise, it’s basically the Pixel 9A, with the same Tensor G4 chip and a dual-camera system. Read our review.
Asus ProArt P14 (RTX Spark)
The entry point into RTX Spark laptops, the Asus ProArt is a creator-focused MacBook Pro wannabe with a sleek blacked-out design and lovely OLED display. Read our initial Nvidia RTX Spark hands-on.
Fractal Scape gaming headset
There are many gaming headsets out there, but few as elegant as Fractal’s Scape. The PC-focused (but Switch- and PlayStation-compatible) wireless headset offers great sound and includes a wireless charger, and it has easy-to-master physical controls.
Nintendo eShop gift cards
Everyone knows gift cards aren’t the best gift, but with such steep discounts happening on Nintendo eShop credit, you can save a lot on a Switch 2, or games and accessories, if you’re alright with jumping through a couple extra hoops.
Xreal One Pro AR glasses
USB-C display glasses can make travel (or relaxing on the couch) more fun by putting a huge virtual screen in front of your face. Xreal’s One Pro are some of the best out there at displaying content from your phone, tablet, laptop, or portable handheld.
Govee Permanent Outdoor Lights 2
Govee’s Permanent Outdoor Lights 2 are Matter-ready smart lights you can leave up year-round. They can display multiple colors at once, with 100 preset lighting scenes, customizable effects, and the ability to sync to music. The lights also feature an IP67 rating for dust and water resistance.
Ecobee Smart Thermostat Premium
The Ecobee Smart Thermostat Premium is an excellent option for adding smarts and some style to your HVAC system. As well as being a smart way to control your energy use, the thermostat can also act as a video intercom for Ecobee’s excellent doorbell camera and an indoor air quality monitor. Read our review.
Cricut Joy 2
The Cricut Joy 2 is a small crafting machine designed for smaller projects, including custom cards, stickers, vinyl decals, labels, bookmarks, and iron-ons. It can cut designs up to 4.5 inches wide and brings Cricut’s Print Then Cut feature to its entry-level lineup. Read our review.
Amazon Echo Time
Although it’s not Amazon’s first bedside alarm clock, the Echo Time is focused on helping you sleep better. The camera-less Alexa speaker can detect your sleep stage via ultrasound and use smart alarms to ease you into the day, but only if you want it to.
The90 Gem
The90’s Gem is a UV-tracking necklace that measures UVA and UVB exposure throughout the day. Its subscription-free companion app tracks exposure trends, offers sunscreen reminders, and uses an optional skin profile to estimate sunburn risk and vitamin D production from sunlight. Read our hands-on impressions.
Reolink Video Doorbell PoE camera
Power over Ethernet provides this 2K resolution video doorbell with rock-solid connectivity while reducing the number of wires you need. There’s no subscription required to view recorded video; it can record locally on a microSD card, Reolink Hub, or FTP server and connect to a platform like Home Assistant.
8BitDo Pro 3 Wireless Controller
The Pro 3 features swappable ABXY face buttons and joystick caps, providing players with a highly customizable experience. It also features new L4 and R4 macro buttons between the triggers and its USB-C charging port, along with more durable and power efficient TMR joysticks.
Camp Snap 2 digital camera
Camp Snap’s latest digital point-and-shoot camera may still lack a screen and capture only 8-megapixel stills, but it offers a slimmer design, faster performance, and filters right out of the box. That, along with several other new features, makes it easier for kids to use.
Govee Table Lamp 2 Pro X Sound by JBL
This RGB smart lamp packs a JBL speaker inside to combine snazzy lighting effects and decent sound into one fun, portable package. Battery-powered and with support for Matter, this is a smart light with party speaker aspirations. It’s the perfect size to add a little punch to your next gathering or snazz up a college dorm room. Read our review.
Eve Energy Smart Plug (Matter)
This smart plug offers the most detailed energy monitoring of any we’ve tested. It supports Matter over Thread and is a good choice for Apple Home and SmartThings users, as it offers energy monitoring on those platforms.
Sonos Era 100 SL
The Era 100 SL is a more affordable version of the Sonos Era 100, just without a built-in mic. Otherwise, it uses the same speaker system for bass-rich sound. It also supports Bluetooth audio and line-in playback via an optional adapter.
Roborock Q10 S5 Plus
Despite lacking a multifunction dock, the budget-friendly robot vacuum and mop offers an impressive set of features for the price, including AI-powered obstacle avoidance, sonic mopping, automatic mop lifting, and a self-emptying dock.
Update, November 28th: Added a couple of new deals, including a good sale price on the unlocked iPhone Air, the MSI Claw with the Z2 Extreme, and a pair of Sonos Era SL speakers.

articles.title: Diablo II
articles.body:
[Diablo II] is a progression with a character where you go and defeat enemies and get rewarded. There’s overriding goals as well as lots of sub-goals. There’s many things to do, yet it’s very simple. It’s very straightforward. There’s no, “What am I supposed to do now?” It’s pretty much in your face as to what you’re supposed to be doing. It’s very easy to click, and it does things automatically…
— David Brevik
There’s never enough blood and fire.
— Max Schaefer
Within a few weeks of the release of Diablo, it was clear that Blizzard Entertainment had a hit on their hands. Within a few months, it was clear that this was more than a hit: that it was another era-defining game from the company that had given the world Warcraft II only a year and a half earlier. Not to make a sequel once that realization had dawned would have been to leave a dump truck full of money parked on the curb.
Fortunately, it wasn’t hard for Blizzard’s upper management to convince David Brevik, Max and Erich Schaefer, and the rest of their team at Blizzard North to throw themselves into such a project. They saw Diablo II as a chance to implement all of the things they hadn’t had the time or resources for back when the first game was an unproven shot in the dark, as well as to fix the infelicities that had cropped up once players had gotten their hands on it in the wild. In their minds, this was to be Diablo 2.0 as much as it was Diablo II.
Yet they knew that they had to tread carefully as they made their improvements, lest they lose the qualities that had made the first game so popular. Diablo I had homed in relentlessly on a simple gameplay loop of (minimal) effort and (maximal) reward: go into dungeons, kill monsters, collect loot, and level up. Rinse and repeat, until you reached the sixteenth dungeon level out of sixteen, beat the last boss, and won the game. Story and setting, strategic and tactical nuance, and all of the other complexities that normally went into the CRPG genre were curtailed or eliminated entirely in homage to the loop, Brevik having intuited — correctly, as the sales figures showed — that a lot of gamers didn’t actually care about that stuff. A sequel which reintroduced too many of the very elaborations that Diablo had pared away risked no longer feeling like Diablo at all, a danger of which the team was well aware.
Thus the three years it took them to make Diablo II were filled with a lot of hand-wringing and second-guessing about how much additional complexity was too much. “In hindsight it feels like it was all fine, we got to where we got, why were we ever worried about it?” says character artist and dialog writer Phil Shenk. “But in the middle of it, yeah, there were times that we felt like we were messing with the formula or that we were ruining it.” They learned to evaluate every mooted change through the lens of a single mission statement: “We aren’t making a CRPG. We’re making a Diablo.”
Shenk was one of about 40 people who joined Brevik and his 20 or so colleagues who had helped to create Diablo I. Despite the tripling of manpower, it took them far, far longer than anticipated to finish the sequel. Those three years were a period of rapid change in the games industry, marked by consolidation in terms of both publishers and gameplay formulas. It is a measure of Blizzard’s enormous success and influence that two of the three most popular such formulas could be traced back to that company: there was a flood of real-time-strategy titles seeking to duplicate the sales figures of Warcraft II, and a flood of so-called “action RPGs” trying to do the same for Diablo. As the turn of the millennium approached, the industry as a whole was increasingly the one that Blizzard and id Software — the inventor of the first-person shooter, the third hugely popular gameplay formula — had made in their image. The new heart of the market was fast-paced, violent, action-oriented in every sense of the phrase, and readily amenable to the online multiplayer matches that were becoming more and more of a priority for hardcore gamers as the state of Internet connectivity steadily improved.
Yet even Blizzard wasn’t entirely insulated from the more worrisome aspects of change and consolidation. Rather oddly in light of the company’s outsized influence as the most successful single studio and publisher of the age, Blizzard was not an independent entity. From 1994 until 1996, it had been owned by Davidson and Associates, a staid specialist in educational software. In June of 1996, it had been acquired along with its parent company by CUC, a strange and voracious shopping-club empire reigned over by a snazzily attired gentleman named Walter Forbes. Along with Blizzard, CUC had also picked up the venerable Sierra On-Line, thus capturing a prodigious chunk of where gaming was going and where it had been in one fell scoop. In December of 1997, CUC merged with an administrator of hotel, rental-car, and real-estate franchises called HFS to form a new conglomerate called Cendant Corporation. Just a few months later, the wheels came off.
Much of Blizzard North was on a junket to Las Vegas when the news broke in April of 1998 that something was rotten in the state of Cendant. “We’re in this hotel room, and all these panicked calls start coming in,” says David Brevik. “We turn on the news, and the number-one story is the Cendant scam. It was ridiculous. We were just watching the stock drop. It was painful.” It turned out that Walter Forbes had had a better knack for accounting fraud than he had for running shopping clubs.
The collapse of Cendant became the biggest American business scandal of the decade, with Blizzard, Sierra, and the rest of the conglomerate’s thoroughly misplaced games division dragged through the mud as unwilling hostages. Ironically, the scandal broke at virtually the same instant that Starcraft, Blizzard’s next mega-hit, was shipping from the publisher’s more southerly offices.
For Sierra, a traditional specialist in adventure games whose products had fallen badly out of favor, the stakes were existential, and in the long run extinctionary. For Blizzard, the hot new whizz kids of the industry, they would prove less serious, for all that you might have had difficulty explaining that to the many Blizzard employees who had dutifully invested a portion of their paychecks into now-worthless Cendant stock. On November 20, 1998, the entirety of the spiraling Cendant games division was picked up by the French conglomerate Vivendi. Everyone understood that Blizzard was the real prize, the once-mighty Sierra merely the baggage that went along with the deal. And indeed, Sierra’s operations would soon be shuttered, the name allowed to live on as a brand only — and soon enough not even that. Blizzard, however, was permitted to continue with business as usual. For even the officious executives at Vivendi knew better than to kill the goose that just kept on laying golden eggs. Not only was Starcraft well on its way to becoming Blizzard’s best-selling game yet, but Diablo I and Warcraft II continued to sell better every single month than the vast majority of brand-new titles from other publishers, their appeal extended indefinitely by Blizzard’s pioneering Battle.net online matchmaking service, which meant that a quick pickup game with a real human was never more than a few mouse clicks away.
Over and above even Battle.net, the not-so-secret recipe for Blizzard’s commercial winning streak was the combination of a laser-sharp attunement to the desires and priorities of the typical young male gamer with an uncompromising commitment to execution and polish in service to those priorities. Blizzard’s staff, both in the North and the South, understood their customers so well because they were their customers, even as they worked so hard to make their games as good as they could possibly be for the same reason. Business itself was a kind of grand multiplayer game to them; the last thing they wanted to do was release a bad and/or poor-selling product that would spoil their winning streak. Thus their willingness to tear everything up and go back to the drawing board on a project, as they did early in the development of Starcraft, or to abandon entirely projects that had begun to seem out of tune with the gamer zeitgeist, as they did a Warcraft adventure game when it became clear that that dog just wasn’t hunting anymore. (Witness: the fate of their Cendant stablemate Sierra.)
Still, the wiggle room that the ongoing success of Diablo I gave Blizzard North as they worked on the sequel only extended so far. The last eighteen months of its development — fully half of the project’s total duration — was one brutal, endless crunch that became a bit much even for these hardcore souls. “It was, to this day, the worst crunch I’ve ever experienced on any project,” says programmer and sound designer Jonathan Stone. “It’s not something you want to keep doing into your thirties.” “You just don’t tell people to work twelve hours a day. It’s really taxing,” says programmer Peter Kemmer. “It drove me out of the company, and I’m sure it drove other people out, because there’s only so much of that you can take.”
The relatively small minority of the Blizzard staff who were married or in serious romantic relationships suffered particularly. Several divorces and breakups resulted from the crunch; among these casualties was David Brevik’s marriage. An older and wiser version of Diablo’s primary mastermind is now all too aware of what his brainchild cost him as well as what it gave him, especially when it came to his relationship with his two daughters: “It scarred me for a long time. It had huge ramifications on my life, most of them pretty negative. It was extremely costly.” Even Max Schaefer, who as a member of the Blizzard North management team was one of the primary drivers of the crunch, has come to recognize that he may not have done his employees’ physical and mental health any favors: “Six months into this crunch period, you’re still going, and you’re not really close to being done, although it always seemed like you were two or three months out. You start to physically and mentally burn out.”
In such circumstances, the colleagues with whom you were spending upwards of 80 hours per week became the sum total of your social life. “Everyone I knew at Blizzard became my circle,” says tester Josh Kurtz. “It became my support structure, my family. I did everything with them.” It was the ultimate recipe for instilling the very same hardcore monoculture, all but impenetrable to outsiders, that Blizzard was making such hay out of serving. Although David Brevik had famously told the team who worked on Diablo I that it should be straightforward enough for their moms to pick up and play, it’s safe to say that not too many mothers were playing Blizzard games out there in the real world. Meanwhile the crunch cycles that made a job in the games industry incompatible with a balanced family and social life did indeed serve to drive most people out of it by the time they reached the end of their twenties, further reinforcing the sense of stultifying sameness that so marked the values and aesthetics of computer gaming during this period. The so-called “casual revolution” of the aughts was partially a response to the “gamerdark” vibe of outfits like Blizzard, offering up a vision of gaming that was at least markedly different, if not always more broadminded, in its own values and aesthetics.
In the here and now of Y2K, however, the hardcore monoculture was capable of generating outsized amounts of money if you hit it just right, as Blizzard had a better aptitude for doing than anyone else. By the time Diablo II was finally pronounced done in June of 2000, its predecessor had sold a cool 2.5 million units and was still prominent on the shelves of every games store in the country, despite its age of three and a half years — donkey’s years in gaming terms. Other action RPGs like Darkstone, Revenant, and Nox — everyone seemed to be searching for punchy one-word titles like Diablo — had shifted their fair share of units as well, although none had come close to matching their primary inspiration’s numbers. Blizzard was so confident in the sequel’s prospects that they shelled out for an initial production run of 2 million copies before they ever shipped the first box to a store.
That decision proved not to have been overconfident. Far from it. Diablo II didn’t just perpetuate Blizzard’s winning streak; it amplified it. That 2-million-copy run sold through in just six weeks; 184,000 copies were sold in the first 24 hours alone, leading the Guinness Book of World Records to crown Diablo II the fastest-selling computer game of all time. (This record would eventually be broken by — wouldn’t you know it? — another Blizzard game.)
One of the few areas where Diablo II did depart from the established code of hardcore gaming was ironically one of the keys to its sales. In a milieu where young men competed with one another to put together the hottest gaming “rig” in much the same way that their fathers might have competed to own the fastest car, Blizzard kept the system requirements of their games counterintuitively modest. Diablo II ran at a fixed screen resolution of just 640 X 480, the same as its predecessor, and used a fancy 3D graphics card as an optional visual enhancer rather than a baseline requirement. It could run acceptably well on a 233 MHz Pentium I with just 32 MB of memory, specs which some widely available laptops exceeded with ease by the year of its release. If you wanted to feel up with the times in gaming but you couldn’t afford to buy or build an expensive wundermachine, Diablo II was the answer to your prayers. You could jump on Battle.net and make a name for yourself without anyone having to know you were borrowing your mom’s work computer.
