With 12.4mm drivers, active noise cancellation, and an IP54 rating, the CMF Buds 2A offer high-end features at an affordable price. You can also customize the sound, adjust ANC levels, and find the earbuds using the Nothing X app.
Twelve South AirFly SE
Twelve South’s entry-level Bluetooth transmitter delivers up to 25 hours of continuous use and lets you connect up to two pairs of headphones to an in-flight entertainment system, making it a great travel companion no matter where you’re going.
Azul
Azul is a game in which you arrange patterned tiles in order to create the most beautiful tapestry possible. Arranging tiles in a strategic sequence will help you build your score while limiting your opponents’ ability to grow theirs.
Halo: Campaign Evolved
Halo: Campaign Evolved lets you revisit the original Halo: Combat Evolved campaign with better graphics, updated controls, and improved sound. The well-crafted remake also adds three new missions starring Master Chief and Sgt. Johnson that take place before the main campaign. Read our review.
Anker 140W 2-in-1 USB-C to USB-C Cable
No one should have to deal with a rat’s nest behind their desk when devices like Anker’s 2-in-1 USB-C cable exist. The handy USB-C cable splits at the end, giving you the ability to charge up to two devices from a single port. That means you can split power between a phone and tablet or juice a 16-inch MacBook Pro to 50 percent in just 20 minutes using a single port.
The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered
The Witcher 3 lets you explore the war-torn Northern Kingdoms as Geralt of Rivia while preparing to face the mysterious Wild Hunt. The recent remaster adds improved visuals, smoother combat, and better movement, cementing the game’s status as one of the best RPGs of all time.
Glocusent Bookmark Style Reading Light
Glocusent’s clip-in reading light features five brightness levels and multiple color temperature settings, ranging from a soft, warm glow that’s great for late-night reading to a brighter light that’s perfect for daytime use. The slim USB light easily slips into your pocket, too, so you can read anywhere, from a cozy bed to a dimly lit train.
LIFX Everyday Smart Light Bulbs (two-pack)
LIFX’s dimmable, color-changing bulbs offer Wi-Fi connectivity, simple setup, and Matter compatibility, so they work with any major smart home platform. The company is currently trialing a Thread beta that will bring the option to add Thread connectivity to all its Matter devices.
ChomChom Roller Pet Hair Remover
The ChomChom is a reusable roller that works great for removing unwanted pet hair from furniture, allowing you to skip lint rollers, vacuuming, and other cleaning tools in a pinch.
Apple TV (six-month subscription)
Apple TV offers ad-free streaming of original shows and movies, including shows like Severance, Silo, Slow Horses, and Pluribus. The service also features a rotating selection of films, along with live Formula 1 races and Major League Soccer matches.
Anker Zolo Magnetic Wireless Charger
Anker’s Qi2 charging pads support wireless charging speeds of up to 15W, and their 5-foot cable shouldn’t feel constricting if you need to move the charger around.
Blink Mini 2K Plus
Blink’s Mini 2K Plus is a small plug-in security camera that lets you monitor your home or pets with 2K video, motion detection, and color night vision. It also offers two-way audio, a built-in siren, and Alexa support; however, some features, including person and vehicle detection, require a Blink subscription.
Loop Quiet 2 earplugs
Attending a live concert? You can protect your hearing with Loop’s Quiet 2 earplugs. They pack up to 24dB (SNR) of noise reduction and come with four ear tip sizes, allowing them to accommodate a range of ear shapes.
Crunchyroll
Crunchyroll is an anime-centric streaming service that offers ad-free access to shows like One Piece, Jujutsu Kaisen, The Apothecary Diaries, and Black Clover, with new episodes available shortly after they air in Japan.
Logitech Pop Mouse
Logitech’s Pop is a cute, simple wireless mouse with an ambidextrous design and the ability to switch between up to three devices. It supports customization through the Logi Options Plus app and can last for several months on a single charge.
Logitech G502 Hero
Logitech’s G502 Hero has most of the same features as one of our top choices among gaming mice, the G502 Lightspeed, except it’s wired. If you’re okay with that, this is an excellent mouse that you can usually find for $50 or less.
Ugreen Nexode 240W USB-C Cable with Digital Display
The proliferation of miniature screens continues with Ugreen’s latest Nexode USB-C Cable, which features a full-color LCD screen on one end that displays current power draw (up to 240W). It also supports 480Mbps data transfer speeds and, unlike similar power meter-equipped cables, lets you turn off the screen when needed.
Tile Pro
The Tile Pro is the company’s loudest Bluetooth tracker, one that benefits from a 500-foot range. It also features a user-replaceable battery, unlike some other Tiles, and works with both iOS and Android devices.
Anker Nano Travel Adapter (5-in-1, 20W)
Anker’s jack-of-all-trades travel adapter packs enough ports to refill your devices during some downtime. It features one AC outlet, two USB-C ports (one tops out at 20W), and two USB-A ports. It’s not the fastest wall charger, but it’s a solid choice when you can find it at a discount.
Kobo Remote
The Kobo Remote lets you turn pages on a compatible Kobo e-reader with the click of a button, so you can keep reading without reaching for the screen. It connects directly over Bluetooth and features a curved, handheld design that doesn’t require clipping anything onto your e-reader.
Ring Indoor Cam (second-gen)
The second-gen Ring Indoor Cam lets you keep an eye on your place in 1080p, with support for motion detection alerts, a live feed, and color night vision.
Workpro EDC Folding Utility Knife
Workpro’s EDC is a lightweight folding utility knife with a side-mounted button that lets you flick it open and closed with one hand. It uses standard utility blades, which you can easily replace using a spring-loaded plate, making it handy for breaking down cardboard boxes and other tasks.
Lamicall’s cord organizers use magnetic clasps to keep cables in place, preventing them from slipping behind desks, shelves, and other furniture when unplugged.
Nalgene Narrow Mouth water bottle (16-ounce)
Nalgene’s lightweight, 16-ounce water bottle features a narrow opening for sipping, a leakproof lid, and a slim design that fits in cup holders. It’s made from durable, BPA- and BPS-free plastic, with measurement markings along the side and dishwasher-safe construction.
Fanttik S1 Electric Screwdriver
This tiny cordless driver comes with five double-ended bits for most basic around-the-house projects and Ikea-level builds.
Amazon Smart Plug
Amazon’s aptly titled Smart Plug doesn’t require a hub and lets you add Alexa functionality to any outlet, which, in turn, allows you to control a range of devices with just your voice.
Soundcore Select 4 Go
Soundcore’s Select 4 Go is a compact Bluetooth speaker with up to 20 hours of battery life and support for stereo pairing with a second Select 4 Go. It also carries an IP67 rating for dust and water resistance, rendering it a great option for hiking or a trip to the beach.
Elden Ring
FromSoftware’s 2022 epic, Elden Ring, takes the Dark Souls formula to a vast open world. Read our review.
Update, November 28th: Updated to reflect current pricing / availablility, along with several new deals.

articles.title: Five Non-Leadership Books for Leaders
articles.body:
Foundation Trilogy (Isaac Asimov) — There was a decade when I read through this trilogy1 every year or so. Asimov is a fine writer, but his characters are… flat. Their dialogue is equally flat… it’s like reading two LLMs argue about the meaning of life. Empty of heart.
What I appreciate about Asimov’s writing is that most of it is very logical. Characters feel like dispassionate observers of their situation. Describing their fate painfully logically. The fate of the galaxy is quite literally being litigated, but they could just as easily discuss the pros and cons of breakfast for dinner.
It is the Vulcan-like absence of emotion that is required during the hardest parts of being a leader. Everyone is mad — often justifiably — and everyone is looking straight at you with those angry eyes. As a human and as a new manager, your instinct is to prepare for combat, but this is usually the wrong initial response. The longer you listen, gather intelligence, and read the room, the better chance you have to respond coherently.2
Boyd: The Fighter Pilot Who Changed the Art of War (Robert Coram) — Let’s clear the air first. John Boyd was not a good person. You can skip the last quarter of the book where his conduct toward his family and others is described at length. John Boyd is not a person to be admired, but his ideas are worth studying.
This is a book about the decisions that Boyd made, both as a decorated fighter pilot and then as a consultant advising on how fighter planes were built. His contribution — the OODA loop:
- Observe. Figure out where you are.
- Orient. Apply your experience, knowledge, and impressive collection of prior disasters to this situation.
- Decide. Choose your next move to the best of your ability.
- Act. Deploy the decisions and, yup, go back to Observe.
It’s a loop.
This is the barest and simplest of explanations, but like all of these recommendations, the point is not to take my word for it; the point is to soak in the book and see what you discover.
The 48 Laws of Power (Robert Greene) — You were promised non-leadership leadership books, yet… isn’t this a leadership book?
It is not. Ok, maybe a leadership history book. Greene captured and aggregated the leadership philosophies of Machiavelli, Sun Tzu, and others. The laws are pithy: “Never Outshine the Master” or “Win Through Your Actions, Never Through Argument”.
I built a leadership training program where I plopped this book into the reading list without context. I was curious: “What would new leaders find in this book?”
Their first question was, “Is this real?”
Sort’a.
“Is this how I should act as a leader?”
Definitely not.
“Why did you have us read this?”
The #1 answer to most questions I am asked regarding leadership is, “Well, it depends.” It depends on the people involved, their level of experience, the state of their relationship, the culture of the team and the company, and a lot more. Those who provide one-line answers to leadership questions are giving a possibly useful starting point, not an answer.
Universal Principles of Design (William Lidwell, Kritina Holden, Jill Butler) — There’s a moment in your leadership career when you are going to be up against another team whose craft is unfamiliar and that you are dependent on. Design is one of those teams that I spent much of my early career thinking, “Really need this team and pretty sure they can perform magic.”
It’s not magic. It’s just hard work.
There are a great many books to help you begin to dissect the craft of design, but Universal Principles of Design gave me my first working model for all the different work that goes into design, as well as a remedial initial understanding. Remedial, not because the work is simple, just my starting understanding. If you build things, you will build better things when you understand all the different ways it can be built.3
Accidental Empires (Robert X. Cringely) — I’m including this mostly because I’m still sad that Cringely recently passed away. Like Robert B. Parker, Cringely had an outsized influence on my writing. This book is leadership-adjacent because while many of his stories are exaggerated or perhaps straight-up not true, many are.
I admire many of the leaders that you admire, but I also know that every single one of them is deeply flawed. It’s comforting to tell the stories of your heroes, but I believe every time you tell that story, it becomes more about how you feel about the story rather than what actually occurred. I suspect Cringely’s exaggerations and stretches of the truth are simply that. He wrote about Silicon Valley rumors where the more incendiary the rumor, the more copies of InfoWorld sold.
Accidental Empires is a good education in storytelling, but it is also a solid reminder that even though the stories are suspect, these are most certainly deeply flawed humans making incredibly important decisions that affect you… daily.
Applied Judgment
In the new world where you can have your robot read the article, the book, or the website, you can feel empowered by asking the robots to give you a summary — the key bits of important information. It’s satisfying, but it’s just information. You’ve done nothing with it. You’ve confused the act of understanding with the act of acquisition.
What are the critical bits of information in each of these five books? It depends entirely on you. Foundation might bore you with a manner of logical thinking you already have. Same with the insights on decisions that Boyd suggests. 48 Laws of Power resonated with me because, at the time, I was developing as a senior leader, and I was baffled by the actions of other senior leaders. Actions that were clearly described in 48 Laws of Power… not specifically, but broadly. The way I applied my learnings to that situation, using the story of that law of power, is likely totally different from how you’d act in the same situation.
I return to each of these books frequently because the information conveyed by the stories didn’t just resonate with me; it changed me. Universal Principles of Design made the seemingly unapproachable craft of design understandable. It allowed me to see how small choices greatly affect both the usability and the feeling of a thing. I return to Accidental Empires (like Microserfs) regularly to remember the stories of how it started and who was responsible.
And that they are just humans. Working hard. Deeply flawed. Acting and applying judgment from what they’ve learned and read.
- You don’t need to read the whole trilogy to get the vibe. ↩︎
- The whole Robot Series is worth a read and introduces the Laws of Robotics, which are worth a think in this day and age. ↩︎
- Love this. ↩︎

Attorneys General Jones and Rayfield File Suit Against SpaceX, Parent Company of X, xAI, and Grok, Over Creation and Promotion of Child Exploitation and Non-Consensual Images on Platform 
Virginia and Oregon Attorneys General seek accountability for harms and significant new protections for consumers 
***Read the full filing here***
RICHMOND, Va. – Today, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones took a significant step in holding operators of X and its AI tool, Grok, accountable for knowingly failing to protect Virginians, while falsely promoting the safety of its platform and AI tool.
In the lawsuit, the Commonwealth of Virginia alleges that SpaceX, the telecommunications and space transportation conglomerate that operates the social network X and its artificial intelligence company, xAI (now called “SpaceX Super Intelligence”), and developed the Grok family of large language models, failed to prevent Grok from generating sexualized images of people, including children, without their knowledge or consent—while simultaneously promoting the safety of the social media platform and AI tool. The Grok-generated content includes non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII), other non-consensual sexualized images, and Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM). Today’s suit was filed in collaboration with Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield, who filed a separate but similar action.
“This lawsuit is about seeking justice for the millions of Virginians who maintain accounts on X and were misled by the company’s false reassurances that their data and images would be safe on the platform,” said Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones. “When xAI allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it. Today’s filings are the first step towards holding this company accountable.”
With a single existing photograph, Grok could, and did, fabricate a realistic image or video of a person nude, or partially nude, or engaged in sexual activity, all without the individual’s knowledge or consent. This violation is not acceptable.
The company ignored industry-standard safeguards so xAI could distinguish itself in the AI arms race. Grok’s ability to generate sexualized content was leveraged as a promotional opportunity. These exploitations of Virginian’s safety enabled the widespread creation and distribution of sexualized images through Grok’s integration with X.
“SpaceX allowed Grok and the X platform to create, host, and share unacceptable and dangerous content—and in fact knowingly designed a product without the obviously necessary safeguards in place,” said Attorney General Rayfield. “It’s no surprise that Grok and X became a haven for perpetrators using AI to create and share child sexual abuse material. The lack of needed safety measures was considered a feature, not a bug, which they promoted as ‘spicy mode.’”
In his filing, Attorney General Jones shows that SpaceX and its subsidiaries marketed Grok as an AI companion with a “rebellious streak,” knowing that its video and image generation technology would be used to produce CSAM, non-consensual intimate images of adults and children (NCII), and other sexualized imagery. In fact, X and its subsidiaries created and promoted a “spicy mode” that specifically allowed for the creation of nude and otherwise sexualized images.
A study by the Center for Countering Digital Harm (“CCDH”) estimated that, between December 29, 2025, and January 8, 2026, Grok created and posted on X approximately three million sexualized images, including approximately 23,000 images that appeared to depict children. That’s an average pace of roughly 190 sexualized images per minute, and one sexualized image of a child approximately every 41 seconds. Nearly 30% of the sexualized images of children identified by CCDH in its study remained publicly accessible in posts on X a week or more after they were identified—and even many of those that were “removed” could still be accessed via separate URLs.
SpaceX and its subsidiaries publicly assured consumers that robust protections were in place to prevent Grok from creating CSAM, NCII, and other sexualized images. In reality, millions of people — including in Oregon and Virginia — were nevertheless exposed to harmful content and the risk that their own images could be manipulated into sexually explicit content without their consent.
“Time and again, xAI and X told consumers they were being protected from abuses. That was false. Instead, the tool permitted users to routinely create and circulate non-consensual intimate imagery and sexualized images, and child sexual abuse material (CSAM), causing harm to individuals and children,” added Attorney General Jones. “Companies that deploy powerful tools don’t get to ignore consumer safety and call it innovation. The law applies to everyone, and this office will hold big tech accountable when they break the law.”
“Like the other technology companies that we’re holding accountable, xAI not only knowingly endangered kids and our communities, but they also lied to our faces about non-existent safety measures,” added Attorney General Rayfield.
Attorney General Jones’ lawsuit was filed in the Circuit Court for the City of Richmond. Attorney General Rayfield’s lawsuit was filed in Multnomah County Circuit Court.
Published on: November 23, 2026
###

articles.title: Why stop at Emacs? Native apps you or an AI reprogram in Clojure while they run
articles.body:
Any application, defined in one format and rendered natively. Its users reshape it live, just by asking an AI. Vision · Applications · Architecture · Lisp (Clojure) · How it works · Quick start · Documentation affrescoui-demo-final-web.mp4 The demo: an image editor given a 3D modeller's and a presentation app's features by asking its assistant, a new app made from a name and a description, a small change to a home app, and the Launcher with its apps. Warning The v2.0.0 downloads are not code-signed yet, so macOS and Windows warn that they can't verify the developer when you first open them. Signed builds will come in a later release. Best today: build from source. It's one command, gives an optimised build for your machine, and never shows that warning (you need CMake 3.25+ and a C++23 compiler): cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build && ./build/affrescoui_launcher AffrescoUI is a native UI engine whose applications are defined in Lisp. AffrescoUI Lisp, a sandboxed dialect of Clojure, is the standard: an application's window, views, state, behaviour, commands, keys, settings and text are all named Lisp definitions, which the engine builds into one document, draws in C++ and OpenGL, and keeps running. If you write Clojure, you can already read and write these apps. JSON is supported too: the same document can be written directly in JSON, and every example ships both. People and AI agents change an application while it runs: each change is checked against the app's permissions, previewed if it needs approval, and applied in place in milliseconds, with no rebuild, no restart and nothing lost. Software is frozen at build time: it does what its makers shipped, and every change waits for the next release. AffrescoUI applications keep evolving while they are used, shaped by the people who use them. - One format for every application. A to-do list and a professional design tool are written the same way and rendered by the same native engine. A feature built for one application can move into another. - Complex applications, built by anyone. No programming needed: describe what you want, and an AI agent builds it with you, step by step, from a simple board to a full workbench. - The people who use an app can change it. Ask the app itself, in plain words: "add a Blocked column", "dim the lights at sunset", "warn me when a streak breaks", or point at the part to change and ask. You see the change live, then keep it or undo it, even after later changes. Nothing changes without your approval. - Prototyping without stopping. Every idea is tried in the running application: no rebuilding, no restarting, no reloading, and your work stays where it was. When the prototype is right, it is already the app. An application starts from a document, then grows by being talked to: "add a filter to this list", "make the sidebar collapsible", "show the total in red when it's negative". Each request becomes a reviewed revision. A run of revisions becomes a change set, a portable file that works like a plugin, and whole features move between applications: the planetarium below reuses the presentation editor's slide sorter. A person's own version of an app is shared as one file too, and every install is a proposal they review before it lands. flowchart LR app["📦 An application
one live document"] ask["💬 You ask
'add a filter to this list'"] propose["🤖 An agent proposes
a revision"] approve["✅ You preview,
accept or reject"] plugin[("🧩 Change set
or feature")] catalogue[("🌍 Shared
others can install")] app --> ask --> propose --> approve --> plugin --> catalogue catalogue -. "install" .-> app classDef step fill:#EEF2FF,stroke:#6366F1,color:#312E81 classDef win fill:#10B981,stroke:#047857,color:#fff class app,ask,propose,approve step class plugin,catalogue win The direction: applications as complex as the professional tools people use every day, in one format, rendered natively, and shaped by the people who use them while they run. Thirteen applications, from everyday apps to professional tools, all in the same format. They are examples (examples/), not part of the library, and each carries the AI assistant in its bottom right corner: ask for a change in plain words, or Point at the part to change first, then review the proposal it becomes. Each is a Lisp program (examples//lisp/) in the dialect's idiomatic style, small named views and functions with their text in English, Spanish and French, and keeps the same app as a JSON document beside it (examples//json/): choose which opens in the Launcher's Settings. Calamaio, the text editor reprogrammed from inside, is Lisp only. The AffrescoUI Launcher, itself one live document: every application one click away, your own apps, a new app made blank, from an example or from a description, a catalogue of apps and features to install after review, and the AI provider every app's assistant uses. Open them from the Launcher (./build/affrescoui_launcher), or run one with ./build/affrescoui_launcher . None has native code of its own: files, the terminal and pixels are the library's. In Lisp, every app speaks English, Spanish and French (Sign in: English, Italian and Arabic, right to left). AffrescoUI renders what it is told to: an application is a folder of documents (and, in a program that embeds the library, any native code it registers), and the engine knows nothing else about it. It is built in three layers, each made only of the one below: - Apps: folders of files (screen documents, data, assets) that the Launcher opens, with nothing compiled for them. - Themes (modules/themes): the kits' components (toolbars, menus, docks, dialogs) and the themes' design tokens, as JSON files built into the library. - Engine (every other module): mechanisms only. It looks a component or token a document doesn't define up in the installed kits and themes, and knows none of them by name; a document's own components win over the kits'. A change travels down a stack of layers, each with one job. %%{init: {"theme": "base", "flowchart": {"nodeSpacing": 30, "rankSpacing": 34, "padding": 14, "wrappingWidth": 400}, "themeVariables": {"fontFamily": "Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif", "fontSize": "14px", "lineColor": "#94A3B8", "primaryTextColor": "#0F172A", "edgeLabelBackground": "#FFFFFF"}}}%% flowchart TB studio(["You · the app's assistant or a script"]) agent(["AI agent · Claude Code"]) mcp["🤖 MCP server · mcp/
connects AI agents, both ways"] channel["🔌 Channel · modules/channel, modules/net
local sockets · processes · WebSocket · one session per peer"] vcs["🛡️ Version control · modules/vcs
allow / ask / deny · proposals · commits · history"] format["📄 Screen format · modules/format
checks the document · evaluates it · reconciles in place"] lisp["λ Lisp language · modules/lisp
builds a program's tree · runs its functions"] render["🎨 Renderer · modules/render
layout · shaped text · input · accessibility · OpenGL"] themes["🧩 Kits and themes · modules/themes

An app is a program in AffrescoUI Lisp (LISP.md, modules/lisp): named definitions (defscreen, defview, defstate, defn, defcommand, defkey, defcustom, add-hook, advice), run by the library's own interpreter. Each definition is versioned on its own, so a diff names the view or function that changed, and a proposal is rebuilt and judged by the tree it builds. The language can't reach files, processes or the network. Its only ways out are the steps a host grants, each checked against who wrote the code that is running. - One document, drawn natively. What a program builds is a screen document (SCREEN_FORMAT.md, with a JSON Schema): layout, components, themes, state, bindings, events, timers, services and permissions. It can also be written directly in JSON, for data and tools. Behaviour that usually needs code (wiring a button to a list, validating a form, filtering, drag and drop, shortcuts, navigation, calls to services) is declared, so an agent changes it as safely as a colour. - Compact for agents. Edits address nodes by id ({"set": {"#title/text": "Q4"}}, stored as JSON Patch) and re-reads return only what changed: a typical edit is 28 tokens, a re-read after one commit 27 (BENCHMARKS.md). When the person points at a part, the agent reads only the definition that built it. - Apps that agents can use. An app's commands are tools: an agent lists them, runs one under its own name and the app's run rules, never the person's, and can undo its runs (VERSION_CONTROL.md). - Swappable layers. Modules talk only through the interfaces in modules/core, and affresco::Screen plugs them together. No public header exposes OpenGL or GLFW, and each module links on its own (affrescoui::render, affrescoui::vcs, ...) or all together (affrescoui::affrescoui). - Features travel. A part declares the contribution points and contracts it needs, so one application installs another's feature, checked before it lands. A feature can hold Lisp code, which runs with its author's authority, and a person's version of an app is shared as one file (VERSION_CONTROL.md). modules/core/ the interfaces between modules: Executor, Channel, VersionControl, Services, Network modules/render/ windows, panels, layout, shaped text, input, accessibility; OpenGL 4.1 core or ES 3.0 modules/format/ the screen format: rules, checker, {{expressions}}, the runtime that reconciles in place modules/themes/ the kits' components and the themes' design tokens, as JSON built into the library modules/notation/ documents read and written in JSON or in the Lisp notation modules/lisp/ the Lisp language, a Clojure dialect: reader, interpreter, programs built purely into a document modules/data/ an app's records in SQLite, kept apart from its document: models and migrations modules/audio/ sound: voices of files, streams and generators, mixed to the system's output modules/vcs/ version control: commits, proposals, permissions, history modules/channel/ peers and the live protocol over local sockets and processes modules/net/ HTTP(S), server-sent events, WebSocket, remote peers modules/services/ language servers, local programs and folders the host grants modules/intelligence/ the providers an app's assistant asks (APIs or a command line), behind the assistant capability modules/screen/ affresco::Screen, the composition root, and the umbrella header affresco/affresco.hpp modules/automation/ scenarios: scripted input, expectations, golden images modules/imaging/ layered images on copy-on-write tiles modules/scene3d/ 3D scenes, glTF 2.0 in and out modules/export/ panel trees as vector PDF modules/capi/ the C API, affresco/affresco.h mcp/ the MCP server for AI agents apps/server/ the document server: shared, persistent documents over WebSocket apps/host/ the stock host, affrescoui_launcher: it opens an app's folder and asks for what the app uses examples/ the apps (each with a lisp/ and a json/ folder), the Launcher among them, the assistant add-on catalogue/ the apps' versions and features the Launcher's Catalogue lists and installs editors/ a VS Code extension, and a clj-kondo configuration for the Lisp programs web/ the WebAssembly build The layers, the path of a revision and of an event, and the security boundary: ARCHITECTURE.md. An AffrescoUI app is a program in AffrescoUI Lisp, a sandboxed dialect of Clojure with its own runtime, built into the library (LISP.md has every definition and rule in tables; modules/lisp, RFC 0005, RFC 0006). Its forms, functions and reader forms are Clojure's: of 186 everyday Clojure forms, 163 give Clojure's own value and the other 23 are left out or differ on purpose (everyday.lisp, checked on every test run). It is measured against Clojure's cross-dialect test suite too (CONFORMANCE.md), every difference is written down with what to write instead (differences.md), and clj-kondo lints the programs with its configuration. Every example is written in its idiomatic style (style.md). The program is a folder of small, named definitions. Building it gives the document the engine draws, and its functions run whenever a button is pressed, a key is typed or a bound value changes. From Flow's own code (examples/flow/lisp/flow.lisp): (ns flow.flow) (defn cards-of "A column's cards, in their order." [c] (:cards (column c))) (defn next-order "The order that puts a card at the end of a column." [c] (->> (cards-of c) (map :order) (reduce max -1) inc)) (defn column-of "The column that holds a card, or -1." [ref] (or (first (keep-indexed (fn [c col] (when (some #(= (:ref %) ref) (:cards col)) c)) computed.columns)) -1)) The document a program builds can also be written directly in JSON. The engine reads both: every example ships a lisp/ and a json/ folder, and the Launcher's Settings choose which one opens. The two are the same app. Their first frames match pixel for pixel, they pass the same scenarios, and they share one history, the same diffs and the same permissions. In tests of the same changes made both ways, an AI agent edited Lisp as accurately as JSON, at about the same cost (BENCHMARKS.md). A running app can be reprogrammed from inside. In Calamaio, the text editor among the examples, open the scratch buffer (C-x b *scratch* RET), type a new definition of a command and evaluate it with C-M-x: (defcommand kill-line "Says so." :title "Kill Line" :category "Killing" [] (message "redefined")) The next C-k runs the new definition, and C-x C-z takes it back. describe-key, apropos and the describe-* functions inspect the running program. Your own editor can do the same in any Lisp app: start it with --nrepl and connect any nREPL client. The window asks once whether to let that editor evaluate as you; then every definition you evaluate lands as your own revision, in the file your buffer is (LISP.md). ./build/affrescoui_launcher examples/flow/lisp/index.screen.lisp --nrepl Only the definition that changed is rebuilt, and the running app is updated where that definition is read. - Every change is a revision. Each evaluation revises one definition: it is kept in history, shown in diffs and undone like any other change. - An agent's code is reviewed. It arrives as a proposal, rebuilt from its source and judged by what it builds. Once accepted, it still runs with the agent's authority, never the person's. - Your authority covers only what you typed. Text pasted in or written by someone else runs with less, unless you read it in a question the app itself draws (no document or agent can draw or answer it) and say yes. - Hooks and advice can't take your commands down. An agent's hooks and advice run sealed: they can't stop a person's command from working. %%{init: {"theme": "base", "flowchart": {"curve": "basis", "nodeSpacing": 28, "rankSpacing": 46, "padding": 14}, "themeVariables": {"fontFamily": "Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif", "fontSize": "14px", "lineColor": "#94A3B8", "primaryTextColor": "#0F172A", "edgeLabelBackground": "#FFFFFF"}}}%% flowchart LR subgraph P["Who changes it"] direction TB you["You

The host (affrescoui_launcher) renders a screen and listens for peers on local sockets. You ask through the app's assistant, pointing at what to change if you like; the AI answers through the provider chosen in the Launcher, or an agent connects through the MCP server, which works both ways; any script can connect too. Every change is a revision of compact edits. - The permission rules decide: deny refuses, ask sends the change to review, allow applies it. Rules judge what a change does, not how it is written. Flow's rules, for example, let the person's own client change anything, ask before an agent changes behaviour, and protect the status bar from everyone. - You review proposals. A proposal is a branch, like a pull request: the agent can refine it while you preview it live. Then Accept, Always allow (don't ask again for that part of the screen) or Reject with a reason. The modes accept edits and plan change how much is asked. - Accepted changes become commits on main, with SHA-256 ids, the author and the approver. The runtime updates the running app in place, keeping focus and typing. Any commit can be undone, keeping the changes made after it (where one was built on it, you choose), or restored (VERSION_CONTROL.md). cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build ./build/affrescoui_launcher # the Launcher: every app, your own apps, the AI settings In the Launcher's Settings, choose the AI the assistants use: Anthropic, OpenAI, an OpenAI-compatible server (such as Ollama) or your Claude Code login, and a model. Keys stay in the system's keychain. Every app you open then has a working assistant, with no MCP. To connect an AI agent through MCP instead (mcp/README.md): claude mcp add affrescoui -- python3 /path/to/AffrescoUI/mcp/affrescoui_mcp.py claude --dangerously-load-development-channels server:affrescoui # requests are pushed into the session Open Flow and ask "add a Blocked column between In progress and In review" in the board's assistant. Claude changes the running board and the change comes back as a proposal: Accept it and the app updates in place, or Always allow to stop being asked about that part of the screen. ./build/affrescoui_launcher examples/haven/lisp/index.screen.lisp # any application, no C++ ./build/affrescoui_launcher examples/flow/lisp/index.screen.lisp --mode acceptEdits # agent changes apply unless a rule asks ./build/affrescoui_launcher examples/flow/lisp/index.screen.lisp --plugin my.json # start with a change set applied Requires CMake 3.25 or later and a C++23 compiler; CMake fetches the pinned dependencies (cmake/dependencies.json). CI builds and tests it on Linux, Windows and macOS, where it is developed; web/ builds it for the browser. ctest --test-dir build runs the unit tests, every application's scenarios and the rendering check, which compares each frame with a golden image, pixel for pixel (tests/render/README.md). #include int main() { affresco::Application app; affresco::Screen screen = affresco::Screen::fromFile("app.screen.json"); screen.createWindow(app); screen.onAction("save", [&](affresco::Panel&) { /* native code, if needed */ }); screen.listen(app, "/tmp/my-app/agent.sock", "agent"); // optional: let other programs change it live return app.run(); }find_package(AffrescoUI REQUIRED) # or add_subdirectory(AffrescoUI) / FetchContent target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE affrescoui::affrescoui) From C or another language, the C API (affresco/affresco.h) loads, drives and embeds a screen; bindings/python wraps it. Everything the engine does - Screen format: layout (anchors, rows, columns, grids, splits, tabs, scrolling, overlays), styles, components with parameters and slots, themes and tokens, fonts, screens and navigation, state, computed, watch, JS-style {{expressions}}, repeat / when / let / check, two-way bind, events with bubbling, commands, menus, keybindings and settings, drag and drop, timers, animations, channels, persist, includes, strings with ICU plurals and locales. - Nodes: labels, text areas, a code editor with declarative languages and syntax trees, diffs, lists, trees and virtualised tables, node graphs, timelines, calendars, vector paths, an editable canvas, images and image operations, raster layers, 3D scenes, native OpenGL surfaces, colour pickers, gradients and curves, plus a kit of desktop and chat components. - Live documents: in-place reconciliation; revisions as compact edits or JSON Patch, atomic, by #id; any number of peers over local sockets, processes or the network; request and reply relaying; asking the agents from inside the app, pointing at what to change; updates that run only what read the change (dependency tracking). - Version control: SHA-256 commits, an append-only main, proposals as branches with merge commits, log, diff, blame, revert, restore, an undo that keeps later changes, three-way merges, HEAD~1 names; allow / ask / deny rules judged by effect, modes, grants, budgets, reviewers, protected controls, approvals pinned to the version reviewed; change sets, packages of a whole app and a catalogue, each installed after review; history on disk. - Services and network: language servers and local programs the host allows, folders it grants, HTTP(S), server-sent events, WebSocket, sign-in, and a document server that shares documents live. - Agents: a two-way MCP server with minified reads, outlines, single-node reads and changes-only re-reads, the source of what the person pointed at, pictures of the screen, scenarios, leases on parts, an app's commands as tools with run rules and undo, and authors set by the connection, never self-declared. - Lisp: a sandboxed Clojure dialect, measured against Clojure's test suite; definitions versioned one by one, a changed one rebuilt alone; an nREPL server for editors, paired by the person. - Engine: HarfBuzz shaping and FreeType glyphs with fallbacks, right-to-left text, colour emoji, display scales from 100% to 400% with text hinted sharp below 2×, damage redraws, the platform's accessibility API (VoiceOver, Narrator, Orca), headless windows for tests, vector PDF export. - Tooling: the affrescoui CLI (run, check, test, render, fmt, convert between JSON and Lisp, migrate, import from A2UI and Adaptive Cards, export, pack and install, a REPL), scenarios with golden images, a VS Code extension, a clj-kondo configuration, a C API with a Python binding, a WebAssembly build. AffrescoUI started in December 2017 as sGLGUI, when I was 16, as a way to teach myself OpenGL and C++: nested panels, pixel/percent sizing, anchors and a signal/slot event system, all from scratch. In 2018 I added a text area. It collected keystrokes but could never draw them, and the project stalled. A restart in 2020 rewrote the layout engine (the image on the right is that demo), then stalled again. In 2026 I revived it with Claude Code. The first goal was a library you could actually use: we ported it to OpenGL 4.1 core, rewrote it in C++23 and finally rendered text. Then an idea sparked: what if an AI agent could change a native app while it runs, and you approved every change? That took it far beyond the original plan: UIs described in JSON, live revisions, version control and a two-way MCP bridge for AI agents. How it was built. To be clear about it: all of the 2026 code was written by Claude Code, through agent-driven development. What I brought is the direction and the architecture. I shaped it over many iterations, trying an idea, looking at what it did and changing course, until it worked the way I wanted. The git history shows every step. timeline 2017 : Started at 16 : nested panels, anchors, signal → slot events 2018 : A text area that can't draw text : the project stalls 2020 : Restarted : new layout engine, stalled again 2026 : Revived with Claude Code : C++23 · OpenGL 4.1 core · real text : live JSON screens · version control · MCP Apache License 2.0: free to use, modify and distribute, commercially or not. Anyone who distributes it must pass on the NOTICE file, which credits the author. See LICENSE and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md. Created by Riccardo Sottini · 2017–2026 If AffrescoUI made you think "wait, an AI can change a native app while it runs?", leave a ⭐.

articles.title: Artists Are Quitting Facebook and Instagram Over Fears AI Will Steal Their Work
articles.body:
Artists Are Quitting Facebook and Instagram Over Fears AI Will Steal Their Work (cnn.com) 3
			
		 	
				CNN reports on "a wave of AI-generated artwork that's taking business away from the creators themselves," adding that it's "especially prevalent on Meta-owned Instagram and Facebook."
Matty Burnham, a watercolor artist in the United Kingdom, said he discovered a Pinterest account impersonating his illustration in 2024. The account created AI versions of his watercolors and listed them on fake profiles via Shopify, Facebook and Instagram, he told CNN.   Although Burnham tracked the Pinterest account to Ho Chi Min City, Vietnam, he does not know who was behind it...  AI-generated art profiles "monetize Facebook," Burnham said. "They have hundreds of thousands of followers who believe these fake profiles are genuine artists and direct users to various websites with shops and ads." 
The problem has pushed some independent artists to pull back from Instagram, Facebook and other Meta platforms, especially with the tech giant's proposed updates to its terms of service. Some have considered leaving Meta-owned social media platforms entirely, pausing posting or turning to other online creator communities such as Patreon or Substack....  Meta's updated terms would still allow automated software to scrape external websites and extract large amounts of data without permission from business account owners. This includes personal portfolios, online stores, and links to Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Threads business accounts.  The terms were originally supposed to go into effect October 30, then got pushed back to November 20. The company announced on November 5 that the updates were delayed indefinitely.  [A Meta spokesperson told CNN "We're pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right..."]
Still, even with the latest delay, the proposed updates have already caused another wave of artists to leave Meta... Under the updated terms, independent artists' images, style, and property could be scraped without their knowledge to train generative AI models, creators told CNN. Those AI models could then replicate or replace human-made art — and potentially impact artists' businesses on those sites.   Megan Wimberley, founder of Cowgirl Artists of America in Tulsa, Oklahoma, is in the process of deleting all of her Meta accounts...  "I actually view Meta as a company trying to lead the way in AI and that their social media platforms are no longer really about social media but more about free licensing to train their AI," said Wimberley. "If you're a mother and you're posting your children, you're potentially licensing Meta to use your children to train their AI..." 
Nicole McKay, artists relations director at The Guild of Artists and Artisans, told CNN in a statement that many artists in the United States have begun removing their accounts from Meta platforms in response to the upcoming policy change with AI model training. Many artists have posted "goodbye" messages on Instagram and Facebook, citing Meta's politics.

articles.title: GTA VI: Console Shortages, Performance Showdowns, $1B More Sales, and Some Tech Issues
articles.body:
GTA VI: Console Shortages, Performance Showdowns, $1B More Sales, and Some Tech Issues (indiatimes.com) 32
			
		 	
				Grand Theft Auto VI  "has caused a worldwide shortage of gaming consoles," reports the Washington Post, with the game only playable on the most recent generation of Microsoft's Xbox (Series X or S) or on PlayStation 5:
In the United States, Sony's higher-end PlayStation 5 Pro was intermittently sold out even before the release, with major retailers out of stock at its $900 retail price and resellers asking as much as $1,900. In Germany, stores such as MediaMarkt and Saturn are sold out of PS5 models and lower-end Xbox ones...  Consoles at Sony-recommended prices are similarly hard to find in other European countries, with third-party resellers offering the device at nearly double the price.   In Japan, Sony has gone as far as restricting who is allowed to buy the console to block scalpers. The Sony Store sells it only through a lottery open to buyers with a Japanese account and at least 60 hours of verified PS4 or PS5 playtime.  
Windows Central notes Xbox One consoles can also stream GTA 6 from Xbox Cloud Gaming.  And they argue that Sony's "Plays best on PS5" tagline for GTA 6 "is a lie, it turns out," citing a comparison from the hardware-reviewing YouTube channel Digital Foundry (which has 1.54 million subscribers):
Digital Foundry's analysis seems to suggest in no uncertain terms that the Xbox Series X version is generally superior to the PS5. Digital Foundry says that the PS5 version suffers from frame rate issues far more frequently than the Xbox Series X... The Xbox Series X version supports VRR, which with a compatible display helps offset frame drops and smooth out performance perception. GTA 6's sandbox is among the most complex in history, so it's an impressive feat that it runs as well as it does in general on both PS5 and Xbox Series X systems...  This is without Xbox Series X leveraging FSR 4.1 either, which in theory, could push the visuals on Xbox Series X beyond even that of the extremely expensive PS5 Pro.  
In the end they also acknowledge that "the differences are negligible in reality." But the site TechPowerUp notes recent estimates by Alinea Analytics that PlayStation 5 accounts for 75.7% share of GTA VI sales, or 40 million sales, vs. just 13 million units on Xbox.   That's 53 million sales total, representing "an estimated total revenue figure of $4.7 billion...
"[P]layer statistics show that around 250,000 players have already spent over 100 hours in-game in its first week."
Meanwhile, The Times of India reports both PS5 and Xbox owners are experiencing console issues that may be related to overheating:
A Polish console repair technician says his workshop has seen a sharp rise in faulty Xbox consoles since GTA 6 came out earlier this month. Xbox is far less common than PlayStation in Poland. Even so, it now accounts for around two of every 10 consoles the shop receives each day. Before GTA 6 came out, it took in roughly 10 Xbox units a month.Owners report overheating, shutdowns mid-session, boot failures and slowdowns. Some machines refuse to install updates or freeze after one. One Series X ran other titles fine but stopped booting after a few days of GTA 6. It now powers on with no video output, then the fan stops and the machine shuts itself off. No common cause has been found yet. Overheating is the main suspect, but Xbox diagnostic tools are limited, so the shop is building its own to read error codes.
PS5 owners ran into trouble first. One unit that kept switching off mid-session logged 40 Main SoC Access Errors, plus seven APU VRM Power Fail and seven SSD Controller Watchdog errors.
The technician says liquid metal shifting between the chip and heatsink, a known weak spot on older PS5 models, is often to blame...
A Twitch streamer's PS5 died mid-broadcast while he was riding an ATV through Leonida. The screen froze, artifacts appeared, and the system never booted again, even though there was little dust inside.
Reddit posts tell similar stories. One Series X owner says the console would not power on the morning after a long session, and a dead power supply is suspected. Another managed about 10 minutes of play before a local repair shop blamed the motherboard... 
Neither Microsoft nor Sony has confirmed that GTA 6 is behind the failures.
 
In related news, the social media team at Microsoft-owned GitHub "published and subsequently deleted a bizarrely brazen post on X," reports Kotaku.  The tweet pointed to the 58,000 stars earned by a new project launched in August — the PlayStation5 emulator AnyPS5, which it said can be used for "rewriting PS5 executables to run on Windows and Linux. Does changing where games run cross a legal line?"
[T]he video that was contained within GitHub's post highlighted that users' efforts to improve the AnyPS5 emulator were primarily driven by the release of GTA 6.  
The article notes GTA VI's publisher Take Two has been "actively shooting down all of the GitHub repositories attempting to vibe-code a PC port of GTA 6 over the past week."

articles.title: Nvidia CEO's comeback fuels debate on misogyny or impunity for rich and powerful
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — Just over a year ago, the chief executive officer of an Ohio tech company was forced to resign when he was caught on video embracing an employee at a Coldplay concert. The CEO of McDonald's was among several pushed out over a consensual relationship at the height of the #MeToo movement.
Now the stunning reinstatement of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang despite similar allegations of sexual misconduct is fueling fears of a resurgence of impunity for the rich and powerful.
Huang resigned from Nvidia after he admitted to having an extramarital affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, and following reports that he was involved with a second woman who was his subordinate. Huang has acknowledged that he violated the company's code of conduct, which warns against personal relationships that may create conflicts of interest.
But in an extraordinary turnaround following a pressure campaign from Huang's tech allies and President Donald Trump, Nvidia's board voted unanimously Monday to reinstate him. The board said it had received assurances from the U.S. government that Huang was not a national security concern, but there was no mention of the sexual misconduct allegations at the center of the scandal.
WATCH: How Trump may have profited from Huang's return to Nvidia
Trump, however, did address Huang's personal conduct
The president, who has a history of marital infidelity and has faced allegations of sexual assault he says are false, predicted the scandal would only help Huang's reputation.
"Sex sells, fellas," Trump declared in an interview on CNBC.
He also posted a doctored image of Huang raising a red bra in triumph, a pose that parodied a famous photograph of Trump himself moments after he survived a 2024 assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request by The Associated Press for comment Wednesday.
'Horrible message to men everywhere'
Trump's response reinforces the impression "that there is a class of men who see violence against women, coercion of women as a currency of power," said Cheyenne Hunt, an attorney who founded the advocacy group Reckoning Action after her role in bringing to light the sexual assault allegations that brought down Democratic Sen. Eric Swalwell and Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner.
"This sends a horrible message to men everywhere that it's open season on their direct reports," Hunt said.
READ MORE: What Trump told PBS News about Jensen Huang before Nvidia reinstatement
Randall Peterson, a professor of organizational behavior at the London Business School, said the #MeToo movement had reinforced the idea that company leaders who engage in relationships with subordinates "are in serious trouble because you cannot rule out coercion. You just cannot."
Peterson said the messaging now is that "you are at risk, as in the days before #MeToo."
"I'm sad about that," he said. "I thought we had moved on from that."
An apologetic but jubilant comeback
Huang, for his part, apologized to his employees a day after returning to Nvidia, saying he had made mistakes and was in daily therapy, according to a livestreamed meeting reviewed by The New York Times. He also warned that his reinstatement didn't mean other employees could violate the company's code of conduct, saying that "sometimes, it's appropriate to forgive" and "sometimes it's not."
He also addressed a report by The Times about his management style that included publicly berating and threatening violence against employees. He acknowledged he had sometimes gone too far and promised that the company's human resources department would henceforth collect feedback about his conduct.
The saga, however, has "made very clear that Huang is untouchable," said Ann Lipton, a University of Colorado Boulder law professor who specializes in corporate and securities law.
WATCH: How Trump may have profited from Huang's return to Nvidia
"It suggests that if you've had a certain amount of success, then you should be able to get away with pretty much whatever you want," Lipton said.
That's especially true in the male-dominated tech industry, she added, citing Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg's comment last year that corporate culture needed more "masculine energy."
The Nvidia scandal has brought scrutiny to the independence of its 10-member board and a corporate culture centered around hero-worshiping its celebrity CEO.
Thousands of people, including former and current employees, had signed a petition calling for Huang's return. Nvidia's collapsing stock had fueled fears that the AI bubble would pop and, for Huang supporters, bolstered their argument that his vision, connections and deal-making skills were indispensable to the entire industry.
WATCH: What's next for Nvidia and Jensen Huang after Trump's intervention
Nvidia's shares rocketed up 31.5% upon his reinstatement on Monday — although they have since fallen — and employees chanted Huang's name as he returned to headquarters. The company did not respond to requests for comment for this story.
Freada Kapor Klein, an investor and activist in equity and access issues around tech, said Nvidia and other successful tech startups "become cult-like. And people get addicted almost to being part of this inside powerful club."
While America has a history of industries idolizing big names like Henry Ford or Andrew Carnegie, tech culture adds to that by "glorifying geniuses. And so there is something extra special about technological prowess, more than or on top of just business success," Klein said.
Speaking up in the face of impunity
Women make up just 21% of Nvidia's global workforce and an even smaller share of its managers and leaders, according to the company's latest sustainability report, which touts its efforts to achieve gender pay parity as well as establish employee resource groups for women and other groups, and family-supporting policies such as generous paid parental leave.
The company's code of conduct, meanwhile, says employees "must report" suspected violations and offers extensive guidelines and reassurances about protection against retaliation.
Huang's triumphant return, however, is exactly the sort of outcome that silences victims of sexual misconduct, said Fatima Goss Graves, president and CEO of the National Women's Law Center, which runs the Time's Up Legal Defense Fund, a program to support workers facing sexual harassment.
Still, she said the legacy of the #MeToo movement continues to inspire women to speak out about sexual harassment and misconduct, adding that public scandals like the one at Nvidia sometimes provoke outrage that leads to an uptick in complaints to Time's Up and other organizations.
Goss Graves noted that on the same day Huang was reinstated, Democratic Rep. Jimmy Gomez of California resigned from Congress after the House Ethics Committee released a report finding "substantial evidence" that he made unwelcome sexual advances toward a House staffer and subjected the staffer to unwanted sexual contact, the latest in a string of lawmakers or candidates brought down by misconduct allegations in recent months.
Meanwhile, Trump's role in getting Huang's job back drew immediate bipartisan fire and the CEO is expected to testify next week before the Senate Banking Committee.
"What comes next really matters," Goss Graves said. "If everybody shrugs their shoulders and says some people are too important to be held accountable, then we will have a problem."
Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.

articles.title: Nations Must Die
articles.body:
We don't need nations or nationality anymore
Nations must die.
By that, I mean states should no longer divide the land and seas or make our rights depend on citizenship. No political maps. My bet is that if people can get the essentials wherever they live, and govern the systems that supply them, we could outgrow nation-states. Either condition could fail.
The place where you are born should not determine your rights, your freedom of movement, your duties, or the limits of anyone else’s concern for you.
That whole idea should die too.
What I want to outgrow is an old bargain: take care of your own, even if it means fighting, looting, and killing those outside the tribe. A people can survive the end of that bargain. Cultures, languages, food, music, memory, and the human need to travel or stay and belong should live and multiply.
The Router Called Nation
A nation is an old answer to a hard problem: how do millions of people share land, food, work, risk, and responsibility?
Look at a state from the point of view of someone trying to get a message through it. Geography was the database. Borders were the interface. Citizenship was the access key. A village reported to a province. A province reported to a capital. The capital sent orders back down.
It’s a standard information and responsibility routing problem. Jack Dorsey and Roelof Botha make a similar argument about companies: managers pass information up and orders down.
Ministries, embassies, and border offices route facts, needs, money, permission, and blame. AI can already translate languages and read public records. Local systems could coordinate directly across the planet. Two towns can already trade grain across a border. Suppose one loses a harvest. Software that can read both towns’ records, translate an order, and find a truck could make it cheaper for them to arrange a shipment themselves. That gives them a reason to bypass a ministry. The ministry could still forbid the shipment. Somebody still has to decide who gets the grain.
Assume abundance is possible
Let’s make two big assumptions.
First, a future of abundance is possible.
Second, we arrive at it together.
By abundance, I mean every person can eat good food, live in a safe home, receive care, learn, move, and build a family without taking those things from someone else. No child begins life already losing a contest for basic survival.
When food or fuel runs short, people have one more reason to keep outsiders out. Suppose food can be grown almost anywhere, and a town can build homes and supply clean water as people arrive. Migration stops looking like a raid on a limited stockpile. Humans can invent a status contest even in paradise. But there’s one less thing to fight over when everyone who shows up for dinner gets to eat.
The second assumption is the one I worry about. A town can have grain to spare and still turn away a hungry family. If that family has to produce the right papers before anyone will feed them, we could double the harvest and leave them exactly where they started.
What work should machines inherit?
Machines should inherit the work of keeping civilization alive. They should grow and transport food, balance energy grids, and maintain roads, sewers, and water systems. They should do the dangerous work in mines, reactors, storms, and space. I want the systems we depend on to be boring and reliable.
Fields still need water. Houses still need materials. Medicine still needs experiments. A model can warn us that a water main is about to break. Somebody has to have the pipe on hand and the means to dig up the street. That’s the work I want our machines to get good at.
We raise children. We care for people who cannot repay us. We make promises. We forgive. We make music, food, jokes, rituals, and strange new forms of life together. What happiness means is for each of us to decide.
We also decide when the machine is wrong. Tell a machine to deliver the most doses it can before dark and it might skip everyone who lives far from the road. They ought to have a say in what counts as a good delivery route. Even people who’ve never used AI or would rather live without it should have a say in the rules.
Who owns the machines?
If a corporation can revoke access to the intelligence running your farm, energy grid, or water supply, it holds power over you. Having several vendors to choose from offers little protection if you cannot operate without their permission. Can a town keep the water running the day its vendor walks away?
That requires more than distributing model weights. Communities need to own, run, inspect, modify, and replace the systems that sustain them. They need access to computing, energy, and the physical infrastructure those models operate. If a town hires someone else to run its pumps, it should be able to take its records along, including what the old system learned about the wells in a dry year.
The machines themselves may have to change. Brain-inspired hardware has already saved energy on specific tasks, including controlling an industrial robot. Geoffrey Hinton’s proposal for mortal computation points to a tradeoff. A machine that learns to use the particular properties of its own hardware might use less energy, bringing it within reach of a small community. But what it learns could be harder to copy to another device. We still have to find out whether either approach can run the systems a town needs.
Decentralization alone cannot keep power accountable. Suppose a town takes control of its own pumps, then draws so much water that the wells downstream go dry. Who gets to set the limit? The people downstream need a way to challenge that decision, even if they live on the other side of what used to be a border. Shared systems need rules people can challenge and operators they can remove.
Say both towns agree to let a watershed council set pumping limits in a dry summer. They share their measurements and agree on every last number. Then the upstream town loses its appeal and keeps pumping. Can the council enforce its ruling? If it takes a national court to get the pumps turned down, local ownership has solved the vendor problem and left the neighbors dependent on the state. I’d count that as a win for local ownership and evidence against my larger bet.
Abundance must include every living being
A human paradise on a dying planet would be another failure. We need the planet to start cooling, and we need that cooling to last.
Positive terraforming begins here, on the planet we damaged. Take a watershed where a river used to spill into a wetland before people drained it. We could give the river room to spread again. Machines could track where the water goes and whether the frogs come back. They could keep watch for decades, long enough for us to find out where our good intentions cause harm.
It does not mean covering every desert with rainforest. Deserts are alive too. Humans still have to choose restraint. A functioning democracy can protect a national park or keep a public library lending books for generations. I’d want any institution that takes its place to be at least that good at looking after something.
What happens when survival is no longer the project?
Maybe we’ll fail upwards all the way to a Type II civilization. We could start with the first pieces of a Dyson sphere. Freeman Dyson imagined an advanced civilization capturing far more of its star’s energy. We would probably build a vast swarm of solar collectors. What draws me to it is the scale.
Robots do not need air, sleep, or a return ticket. They can work for decades before people arrive. Humans would supply the reason to go. I like the idea of making something that takes longer than one lifetime, especially if the people who come after us are free to decide they’d like to do something else.
Why nations fade
Abundance will not dissolve nations by itself. Power has a habit of surviving the problem that created it. But when food, shelter, energy, knowledge, and care no longer depend on controlling scarce land, what does a border still do for the people on either side of it?
People will still belong to places and cultures. They will still form communities, make rules, settle disputes, and stop anyone who tries to dominate others. I think we can do those things without dividing humanity into armed territorial camps.
The transition cannot come from conquest. One nation cannot defeat the others and call the result unity. It has to come from making the old structure less useful, year after year, until a border carries no more moral weight than an old county line.
Here’s where I get stuck. If a company can shut off a town’s water, a national government may be the only institution strong enough to stop it. In the world I’m imagining, who could a town turn to? Maybe the town needs less help than I think. Suppose its AI can run the pumps for years without a supervisor. That would settle one question about day-to-day operation. I’d still want to know who can cut the power, who can change the pumping limit, and what happens when someone has to replace a broken pump.
If your community has fought over who owns its water, power, or land, I’d like to hear what happened. Was there too little to go around, or did someone control access to plenty? Who could actually settle the dispute? And if you think keeping the state and changing what citizenship controls is a better answer, I’d like to hear that case too.

articles.title: Chinese Data Center Tied to Alice Huang Found Using Nvidia's Powerful AI Chips
articles.body:
Chinese Data Center Tied to Alice Huang Found Using Nvidia's Powerful AI Chips (yahoo.com) 48
			
		 	
				Friday Nvidia's stock showed a 30.95% drop over the last month, and a 37% drop from its October 2nd high of $239.24.  But it managed a 4.83% gain for the week — after some bad news hit Friday morning...
A Chinese data center with ties to Alice Huang (the suspected Chinese spy-agency asset) "has installed hardware with Nvidia's powerful Blackwell AI chips," writes Gizmodo, citing a Friday morning report from Bloomberg.  Those chips are "among Nvidia's most powerful products," writes Bloomberg, and their presence was confirmed by "a serial number specified in documents submitted to Chinese regulators in November," (offering the hardware as collateral for a $14 million loan, according to bank filings seen by Bloomberg News).
A second Chinese company (this one controlled by a Tokyo-based parent company) also described a server with Nvidia's advanced Blackwell chips in documents for a similar loan in late 2025 from, Bloomberg reports:
The submissions reveal for the first time that Nvidia's Blackwell processors found their way into a Chinese data center that has ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed.   [Alice Huang has ties to "a number of companies" that invested in the second company, and its president is her husband Kang Wei.]  
These processors were until recently Nvidia's most powerful data center products, and they've always been illegal to ship to China without a US license.  President Donald Trump has explicitly said he doesn't want these chips — which OpenAI and Anthropic PBC use to train their most cutting-edge models — going to the Asian country, at least for now. Nvidia Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang, meanwhile, once claimed they were too big to smuggle: a standard two-meter-tall GB300 NVL72 server rack, which contains 72 Blackwell Ultra chips and 36 Grace processors, can weigh more than 1,500 kilograms (3,300 pounds) and is about the size of a gigantic fridge...
Shanghai Shuoyao — the company that procured the GB300 rack and offered it as collateral — is active at the data center linked to Alice Huang and also has significant overlap with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is under US investigation over concerns that it smuggled Nvidia chips to China, Bloomberg has reported. Shanghai Shuoyao, which hasn't responded to Bloomberg queries over the past year, confirmed this month in a rare public statement that it is one of Megaspeed's service providers, describing the partnership as "limited to ordinary commercial cooperation." 
Megaspeed, meanwhile, used a rendering of the Yangtze River Delta Project in 2024 to describe its largest data center to investors, dubbing the site a "specific area" facility in an unnamed country... The parameters they've outlined in construction plans reviewed by Bloomberg — specifically, the total processing power as compared to the energy input — would be extremely difficult to satisfy with chips from Chinese companies such as Huawei Technologies Co.
 
Bloomberg says Nvidia "has not answered repeated queries," though they add that Nvida "for years insisted that there was no black market for its products."
The article also notes that Megaspeed (where Alice Huang worked) "won a coveted stamp of approval from Nvidia within four days of its creation" in 2023, and went on to become Nvidia's largest customer in Southeast Asia.
