articles.title: My favorite MPC beat maker is ready for your vibe-coded firmware and effects
articles.body:
Akai is continuing to open up its various music-making platforms with the MPC Sample 1.4 firmware. My favorite (and the most affordable) of the MPC samplers has become a popular home for vibe-coded custom firmwares and mods. The company has decided, rather than fight it, to embrace the modding community. The latest update adds several new developer features, including support for the new SDK and custom Knob Effects plugins.
My favorite MPC beat maker is ready for your vibe-coded firmware and effects
MPC Sample 1.4 officially opens up the device to modders and third-party developers.
Plugins added to the appropriate folder on your microSD card are now automatically recognized and will appear at the bottom of the list in the Knob Effects menu. There’s also a Developer Mode, which lets you run scripts from the microSD card or access the sampler’s internal filesystem over USB, which will be handy for all those modders vibe-coding their own add-ons for the MPC. There’s also remote screen access for mirroring the display on an external monitor through the MPC Remote Screen Viewer app.
There are a few other nice updates, including flatten pad, which speeds up the resampling process for baking in effects on individual pads, and sequence record autoplay, which adds a looper-like experience. Akai also added a scale option to the 16-levels pad mode, so you’re not limited to 16 chromatic notes, and can instead play melodic one-shots in E minor pentatonic, B major, or whatever key your track happens to be in.
For a look at some of the custom firmwares, effects, and other mods already available for the MPC Sample, check out this video from Loopop.

articles.title: UK net migration at lowest level since 1997
articles.body:
UK net migration at lowest level since 1997 as asylum claims also fall
Net migration to the UK has fallen to 77,000 in the year to the end of June - the lowest level this century, other than during the pandemic, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures show.
Excluding the limited movements of people during the worldwide travel restrictions in 2020, the figures show the number of people arriving in the UK, minus those leaving, tumbled 92% from the record high of 944,000 in the year to March 2023.
The ONS said this was the lowest net migration since 1997.
Net migration is a measure of how many extra people are added to the population in a given year.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures showed there was now "a sufficient degree of control" over the migration system.
The prime minister went on to say: "I'm not going to say all of the work is done, and I don't want to appear complacent, but I think we're finally as a country getting into the position that the public has long wanted to see."
The underlying official statistics show that an estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June while 661,000 emigrated.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the figures showed that Labour had "delivered" after Conservative failures - but Chris Philp, her Tory shadow, said restrictions introduced by his party before the 2024 General Election were behind the falls.
The 77,000 figure is also the first time the UK has seen net migration in the tens of thousands since former PM David Cameron's controversial pledge 16 years ago to reach such a level.
The biggest factors in Thursday's record low were falls in the arrivals of people coming from outside Europe in three major categories of migration: The number of people coming to the UK to work fell by 45,000, asylum claims fell by 19,000 and the total number of students fell by 33,000.
These number had been expected to fall because of the tightening of visas rules that began under the previous Conservative government which was then continued by Labour from July 2024.
The effect of those policies, plus emigration from the UK, has meant that while net migration had already begun to fall, it more than halved in the last 12 months alone.
Mahmood said the figures showed the government had "restored control".
"We have brought net migration to 77,000, down 92% from its peak under the Conservatives," she said. "Where they failed, we have delivered for the British people."
This is a reference to the so-called "Boriswave" after Brexit. When the UK left the EU and its freedom of movement rules, Boris Johnson's government allowed in many more people to work and study from other parts of the world.
That led to the record-breaking arrivals in the year to March 2023. Johnson's successor, Rishi Sunak, introduced major restrictions on visas in the last months of his government.
Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the falls were a result of those changes.
In a post on X, he called for an "annual legally binding inward migration cap, set by Parliament, at far lower levels".
Dr Ben Brindle of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, an impartial expert body, said: "We are entering an unusual period where immigration has come down and may still have further to fall - but we still have relatively high emigration, at least for the time being.
"Most of those emigrants are non-citizens, including people who arrived a few years ago when immigration was very high. That could push the net migration figures down even further next year, but the downwards blip is unlikely to last forever."
In the year to June some 73,000 people arriving in the UK seeking asylum - down from 93,000 the previous year.
As of September, the number of people who were waiting for a decision was 41,000, down 49% on the previous year.
The Home Office said that these changes were driven by speeding up the system in taking decisions and a fall in the arrivals of new claimants via "illegal entry routes" - largely meaning English Channel small boats.
As a result, the number of people accommodated in September by the Home Office was 93,000 - 16% lower than the year before. Some 52 hotels that had been dedicated to asylum seekers have been emptied this year. While some 140 are still in use the total number of people in hotels has fallen 64% to 13,000.
Responding to the latest statistics, Reform UK's home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said the figures were "no cause for celebration".
"This population explosion is why British people struggle to get a GP appointment, can't get housing and our prisons are overwhelmed."
Liberal Democrat asylum and immigration spokesperson Paul Kohler said: "Britain faces serious demographic and economic challenges, and urgently needs a proper immigration plan to support our economy and public services."
A spokesperson for the Green Party added: "Creating a harsh environment for migrants and people seeking asylum is not a measure of success. The British people are overwhelmingly compassionate and will not be taken in by the dangerous and opportunistic narratives of the far right."

articles.title: Prospero: Bloat-free, native AI coding harness with ImGui
articles.body:
Prospero is a native GUI application for Windows, macOS, and Linux that connects to an AI model provider, local or remote, allowing AI agents to drive your computer to develop software. It plows through intermittent errors and keeps at its task while unattended. It speaks the OpenAI Chat Completions API, used by llama.cpp, vLLM, LiteLLM, and providers with a compatible API. Also Anthropic's Messages API, with extended thinking and prompt caching. No providers are configured out of the box.
The UI is highly flexible, and you can rearrange the panes as you please with dragging and docking. Save your layouts for later in View -> Layouts. Unlike conventional ImGui applications, rendering is passive and will not consume resources while idle.
It is a single executable, written in C++. In the typical case the engine runs in the same process as the window, and needs no daemon or server. The same executable can run headless, on another machine over ssh, or in the background after its window closes. The engine is lean and portable, and runs on computers and operating systems a quarter century old. Imagine a coding harness on Windows XP.
Once it's connected to a provider, you can ask Prospero for help with itself. It will read its own embedded documentation, self-configure, and navigate you to any place in its UI.
Prospero's desktop control features allow it to effectively develop, test, and debug native GUI applications. On Windows, it especially works well in w64devkit, making use of its shell and tools if available.
You can start new sessions from the command line, even if there's already an instance, by invoking Prospero with a path where the new session will be rooted. For example, to start a session here:
$ prospero .
After no arguments, this is the second most common way to run Prospero.
- Usage: running it, sessions, the GUI, attachments, modes and the command line
- Configuration: prospero.ini, endpoints,
models, roles, instructions, skills, MCP servers and web search
- Desktop control: letting the agent see and drive the screen
- Remote and background hosts: engines on other machines over ssh, and sessions that outlive the window
- Windows notes
- Building: building from source, and releases
- Development: tests, and evals for comparing models
Prospero also carries its own documentation, under Help, which an agent in it can read too.
Prospero is free and unencumbered software released into the public domain. See UNLICENSE.
Its programs include third-party code under its own licenses: Dear
ImGui (MIT), FreeType (FTL), md4c (MIT), SDL3 (zlib), cpp-httplib
(MIT), Mbed TLS (Apache-2.0), and Wuffs (Apache-2.0 or MIT, at your
option), which every program with the engine includes. The built-in
model's network, src/gemma.cpp, is derived from gemma4.c and stays
under its MIT license.

articles.title: The AT&T Unix PC (3B1) VM
articles.body:
(This is a guest post by Tenox)
The AT&T UNIX PC, aka PC 7300 aka 3B1, is a 1985 Unix desktop developed by Convergent Technologies and sold by AT&T. Emulating it is nothing new. Phil Pemberton started FreeBee in 2010, and Neozeed has covered it here since: booting the diagnostic disk in 2011, booting AT&T UNIX in 2014 thanks to Andrew Warkentin, and running the C compiler in 2020 thanks to shadyjesse. Arnold Robbins added bigger disks and keeps the 3B1 software alive at skeeve.com/3b1. However there was no networking, and the mouse had to be grabbed with F10.
Now it all has been patched up in my fork of FreeBee:
- Ethernet and TCP/IP! The 3B1 Ethernet board, borrowed from MAME (Visionik‘s 3B1 board and Patrick Mackinlay’s LANCE), on libslirp. Wollongong’s WIN/TCP does telnet, ftp and rsh, out to the Internet.
- Seamless mouse! No more F10 grab. The pointer just moves in and out of the window, and the scroll wheel works!
- Turbo and CPU idle! 10x as fast as a real 3B1 (1x to 32x), with the clock in real time. And an idle VM now takes about 4% of a Mac core instead of 44%.
- Fixes! No more frozen Office forms, stuck Alt key or flicker on macOS.
- Scripting! A control socket and an MCP server.
It’s all in a pull request to Phil’s upstream FreeBee, still open: https://github.com/philpem/freebee/pull/57, and the CPU fix in one to his Musashi.
The ultimate UNIX PC image! UNIX System V 3.51m with Fix Disk 2.0 and 187 packages: nearly every program made for the UNIX PC, like Microsoft Word, Multiplan, dBASE III, WordStar 2000, GCC 2.5.8, GNU Emacs 19, TeX and over 80 games. It comes from THE STORE!, the 3B1 archive and the disk images of Arnold Robbins, Alain Knaff and the VCF. Credit is due!
Behold! UNIX System V 3.51m and the Office on an emulated AT&T UNIX PC:
Specs: AT&T UNIX PC (3B1), 68010 at 10 MHz (10x here), 4 MB RAM, 720x348 one-bit screen, 195 MB disk, 3B1 Ethernet board
Everything runs in windows that you move, resize and overlap with the mouse, even the system panels:
Let’s look at some cool apps!
The Demonstration Programs are pure eye candy:
There are productivity apps too! Microsoft Word and Multiplan take the full screen:
Now some new stuff, made in 2026 for this image!
New Games! 2048, Bubble Breaker, Falling Blocks, Snake and Sokoban, all AI generated, as native 3B1 windows in the Office:
telnetu! The old WIN/TCP telnet chokes on today’s servers, so I wrote a new one with its own VT100/xterm terminal, UTF-8 and DNS, full screen or in windows: https://github.com/tenox7/telnetu
Archaic! A tiny web browser for WRP, which renders the page on a modern computer and sends it as a picture with clickable links: https://github.com/tenox7/archaic
Bonus: the tall screen! Just for fun I patched FreeBee, the kernel, the window driver and the shared library to run at 720×696. It’s a super hacky hack, so it has its own branch and image:
As usual I have prepared a ready to run, portable image with FreeBee binaries for macOS (Apple Silicon), Linux (x64 and arm64) and Windows (x64). Just unpack and run run.sh (or run.cmd on Windows). At “Please login:” type tenox for the Office, or root for a shell. There are no passwords. For Archaic, start WRP on your computer first.
Download: https://files.42718.net/mirror/tenox/os/att/3b1/virt/att3b1-unix351-freebee.tar.lz
Tall screen: https://files.42718.net/mirror/tenox/os/att/3b1/virt/att3b1-unix351-freebee-tallhack.tar.lz
Source (FreeBee, my fork): https://github.com/tenox7/freebee
Have Fun with Virtualization!

articles.title: Show HN: Getting 101 tok/s from Inkling 2 Mini in vLLM on one GB10
articles.body:
Getting 101 tok/s from Inkling 2 Mini in vLLM on one GB10
196 tok/s across four concurrent requests, a 9.7-second 32K prefill and room for a second model.
After taking Inkling 2 Mini for a spin on my GB10, I wanted to make it faster without leaving vLLM, removing Qwen3.8-27B from the machine or shrinking Inkling’s 131,072-token context.
A few days of tuning later, Inkling runs at:
- 101 tok/s for a single request.
- 195.7 tok/s in aggregate for four concurrent requests.
- 9.7 seconds to the first token on a 32K prompt.
On tonyd2wild’s Inkling benchmark, that’s the fastest single-request vLLM result I know of. On the same benchmark tonyd2wild’s setup on TensorFold, a separate inference engine, measured 105.5 tok/s. knapcio’s recipe for the SGLang engine reached 112.0. With four requests at once my setup beats both of tonyd2wild’s published setups.
Inkling still uses 36% of the GB10’s memory. Qwen3.8-27B stayed loaded but idle while I measured.
The work covered vLLM settings, speculative decoding, CUDA graphs and the GPU kernels behind Inkling’s experts.
How a request runs on Inkling
A request runs in two phases. Prefill reads the prompt in chunks of 4,096 tokens and produces the first token. Decode generates the rest of the reply, several tokens per step.
Decode uses speculative decoding. A small draft model proposes 7 tokens and Inkling checks all of them in one pass. The rejection sampler keeps the proposals up to the first one Inkling rejects, plus one token of Inkling’s own, so every step keeps 1 to 8 tokens.
Mapping changes against the request path:
Common terms:
The routed experts take 53% of a decode step and 44% of a 32K prefill:
The starting point

Offline test before building:
- I logged the draft probabilities and accepted token counts for 8,600 decode steps.

- Make the modifications reproducible. Pin every overlay file by hash and build each from one exact source file, so an upstream change fails the build instead of quietly changing the service.

  "${OVL_ARGS[@]}" \
  "$IMAGE" \

    --max-model-len 131072 \
    --max-num-seqs 24 \
    --max-num-batched-tokens 4096 \
    --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
    --safetensors-load-strategy eager \
    --speculative-config '{"method":"dflash","model":"/models/Inkling-2-Mini-DFlash2","num_speculative_tokens":7,"kv_cache_dtype":"auto","draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}'
OVL_ARGS holds the read-only mounts and these switches.
The full launch script, overlay builders and benchmark scripts are in the home-ai-lab repository.

On TensorFold, Mia’s README measures the 4-bit head and verify width adding 33% on code and 18% on prose for one stream at temperature 0. My versions added about 12% on tonyd2wild’s benchmark. The benchmarks differ, but the gap in the size of the gains suggests TensorFold’s versions go further than mine. knapcio’s 112.0 on SGLang shows there is more decode speed to find on this hardware.
Next experiments, prefill first:
- Prefill attention, which took 2.3 seconds of the 32K profile and grows with the context.
- The dense projections, some still on CUTLASS kernels built for Ampere rather than Blackwell.
- A 4-bit copy of the output head for drafting.
- Verifying fewer rows outright instead of skipping their experts, which needs more work around vLLM’s CUDA graphs.
- Verify width for text DFlash2 already predicts well, such as counting.

- Measure the opportunity before building. The logged draft probabilities and the measured cost of a skipped row predicted the verify-width gain before I wrote the runner.
- Keep experiments controlled. Write the acceptance rules before each A/B test, run the unchanged setup before and after each candidate, hash the temperature-0 output of fixed prompts and run probe prompts.
- On unified memory, watch the other models. One run that overlapped Qwen3.8-27B activity saw Inkling’s counting speed halve, so I discarded it.
- Make the modifications reproducible. Pin every overlay file by hash and build each from one exact source file, so an upstream change fails the build instead of quietly changing the service.
Running the configuration
The setup uses vLLM’s inkling-2-mini container image pinned by digest, with the Inkling checkpoint at revision ed40e7da625f.
The changes are eight files mounted read-only over the image. They add the DFlash2 patches, sxuff’s INT8 kernel, the INT8 draft copies, the compile-stall fix, adaptive verify width and the prefill GEMM configuration. The overlay README lists each file with its source, SHA-256 hash and build steps.
The launch command, abridged:
docker run -d --name vllm-inkling --gpus all --ipc host --network host \
  -v "$MODELS:/models:ro" \
  "${OVL_ARGS[@]}" \
  "$IMAGE" \
  vllm serve /models/Inkling-2-Mini \
    --gpu-memory-utilization 0.36 \
    --max-model-len 131072 \
    --max-num-seqs 24 \
    --max-num-batched-tokens 4096 \
    --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
    --safetensors-load-strategy eager \
    --speculative-config '{"method":"dflash","model":"/models/Inkling-2-Mini-DFlash2","num_speculative_tokens":7,"kv_cache_dtype":"auto","draft_sample_method":"probabilistic"}'
OVL_ARGS holds the read-only mounts and these switches.
The full launch script, overlay builders and benchmark scripts are in the home-ai-lab repository.
What’s next
On TensorFold, Mia’s README measures the 4-bit head and verify width adding 33% on code and 18% on prose for one stream at temperature 0. My versions added about 12% on tonyd2wild’s benchmark. The benchmarks differ, but the gap in the size of the gains suggests TensorFold’s versions go further than mine. knapcio’s 112.0 on SGLang shows there is more decode speed to find on this hardware.
Next experiments, prefill first:
- Prefill attention, which took 2.3 seconds of the 32K profile and grows with the context.
- The dense projections, some still on CUTLASS kernels built for Ampere rather than Blackwell.
- A 4-bit copy of the output head for drafting.
- Verifying fewer rows outright instead of skipping their experts, which needs more work around vLLM’s CUDA graphs.
- Verify width for text DFlash2 already predicts well, such as counting.

articles.title: I'm Scared of AI
articles.body:
I'm scared of AI...
Dear Soapboxers, AI is scaring me, and not for the reason you think. Yes, the threat of increasing hacks that could melt down the global economy or trigger nuclear Armageddon is terrifying...but I can't do sh*t about that. What scares me is what AI is doing to my brain. I think I'm getting dumber every time I outsource my thinking to AI. Everything now takes less effort which sounds great, but there's no sense of achievement from it. I haven't taxed myself and I don't deserve the nice chemicals my brain would normally make if I completed some hard work, so it doesn't give me them. It feels like a use it or lose it situation where I'm losing my ability to brain. I read this last week: https://poeticoutlaws.substack.com/p/the-comfortable-life-is-killing-you which explains what I mean far better than I can (because I'm stupider now). Can anyone out there in the Soapbox hivemind share some advice on how to fix this? Or your own thoughts on it? I can't be the only one...
Written by a randomly drawn subscriber, read by a human, then sent to the whole list. Its writer chose to share it here.

articles.title: Kodak’s adorable Charmera keychain camera is on sale for just $30
articles.body:
We wouldn’t normally recommend a bad camera, but we’ll make an exception for the Kodak Charmera. As my colleague Andrew Liszewski pointed out in his review, the tiny retro keychain camera takes pretty lackluster photos, yet it’s charming enough that he kept using it anyway. That makes it a great gift for anyone who loves cute gadgets, especially now that it’s on sale at Amazon and B&H Photo for an all-time low of $29.74 (about $5 off).
Kodak’s adorable Charmera keychain camera is on sale for just $30
The tiny keychain camera is a ton of fun to use, even if its photos are laughably bad.
The Charmera is small enough to carry on your keys and comes in a blind box, so you won’t know which of the six retro designs or the rarer transparent version you’re getting until you open it. It’s a simple point-and-shoot with a tiny LCD screen, and its 1,440x1,080-pixel photos often look fuzzy and washed out. Some of the built-in effects can make the results more interesting, though. Liszewski had some fun with the black-and-white mode and found that the red, blue, yellow, and gray pixel filters could produce bolder two-tone images. Video and audio quality are poor, too, and you can’t adjust much to improve them. Still, for a $30 keychain, it offers a surprising amount to play with.
The Charmera isn’t something you’d want to rely on for an important occasion, but it can be fun to experiment with. Liszewski found that even though most pictures weren’t worth keeping, he’d occasionally get one interesting enough to share. That makes it a fun stocking stuffer for someone who loves cute, unusual gadgets.

articles.title: Roborock, Dreame, and Eufy are cutting robovac prices in half for Black Friday
articles.body:
Black Friday is here, and if you want a little help keeping your floors clean this holiday season, now is a great time to pick up a robot vacuum. Some of the best models we’ve tested over the last year or two are on sale for up to 60 percent off, whether you’re after a basic robovac for quick cleanups or a more advanced model that vacuums, mops, and practically takes care of itself.
The best robot vacuums we’ve tested are up to 60 percent off for Black Friday
From self-cleaning vacs to bots that also mop, you can save hundreds on many of our favorite models.
This year’s sale has made some pricier robot vacuums a lot more affordable. The Eufy Omni C28, for example, now costs about what you’d expect to pay for a budget bot, while the Matic — which impressed us with its almost humanlike navigation — is getting a rare discount in the form of a bundle. If none of those are quite what you’re looking for, we’ve also found good deals on models from Roborock, Dreame, and more, with picks below for a variety of budgets and cleaning needs.
Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 Flow
Roborock’s first roller-mop robot vacuum, the Curv 2 Flow, features flagship specs at a midrange price, including excellent mopping, a retractable mop cover, 20,000Pa suction, AI-powered obstacle avoidance, and a compact design. Read our review.
Roborock Q10 S5 Plus
Despite lacking a multifunction dock, the budget-friendly robot vacuum and mop offers an impressive set of features for the price, including AI-powered obstacle avoidance, sonic mopping, automatic mop lifting, and a self-emptying dock.
Matic robot vacuum
The Matic robot vacuum and mop is ideal for cluttered homes with pets, multiple floors, and a mixture of carpets and hardwood. It offers almost humanlike navigation, tackling high-pile rugs and mopping up wet spills. The quiet bot also requires less maintenance than many rivals thanks to its onboard water tank and dust bag. Read our review.
Eufy Omni C28
The Eufy Omni C28 combines excellent mopping performance with a small self-cleaning dock that’s well suited for apartments and other smaller spaces. It navigates around furniture and into tight areas with ease, while its roller mop does a great job cleaning hard floors.
Dreame X60 Ultra
The Dreame X60 Ultra is a powerful robot vacuum and mop that does a great job of cleaning carpets thanks to its dual roller brushes and 35,000Pa of suction. It can climb over tall thresholds, squeeze under low furniture, and automatically detach its mop pads when vacuuming carpets.
Narwal Flow 2
The Narwal Flow 2 is an excellent robot vacuum for hardwood floors. A superb mop with a wide flat roller pad and a good vacuum, the Flow 2 also has top-notch navigation and obstacle detection. Its sleek base station is also less of an eyesore than most models. Read our review.
Roborock Saros 20
Roborock’s Saros 20 stands out for its ability to climb tall thresholds, avoid obstacles with impressive accuracy, and clean under low furniture thanks to its slim design. It also combines powerful 36,000Pa suction with great spinning mop pads, which is why we recommend it for homes with multiple floor types and tricky transitions between rooms.
Ecovacs Deebot X12 OmniCyclone
Ecovacs’ robot vacuum and mop can pretreat stains, keep carpets dry with a smart mop cover, and deliver powerful 22,000Pa suction. It also includes an all-in-one dock that automatically empties the dustbin, refills the water tanks, and washes the mop with heated, pressurized water.
Switchbot K11 Plus
The Matter-compatible SwitchBot K11 Plus is ideal for small apartments, bedrooms, and home offices. It can easily navigate around chair and desk legs and into tight spaces that most other bots miss. It also features a commendable 6,000Pa of suction power — which is great for this price point — and works well on both hardwood and carpet.
Dreame X50 Ultra
With high suction power, an improved brush system, and the ability to scale thresholds up to 6cm, the X50 Ultra stands out as a great robot vacuum-mop hybrid. While its 20,000Pa suction isn’t quite as powerful as the X60 Ultra’s and it can’t tackle especially high thresholds as well, it’s still an excellent option. Its edge cleaning also isn’t quite as effective as the X60 Ultra’s, but you’re otherwise getting many of the same features for a lot less.
Dreame L40 Ultra Gen 2
The Dreame L40 Ultra Gen 2 delivers powerful 25,000Pa suction, AI-powered obstacle avoidance, and a self-cleaning dock that empties the dustbin, washes the mop, and refills its water tanks. Unlike the X50 Ultra, however, it lacks the ability to climb high thresholds or stairs.
Narwal Freo X Ultra
The Freo X Ultra features spinning triangular mop pads and can swing slightly to reach baseboards. Its large charging dock holds two big water tanks, while Narwal’s disposable onboard bin compresses the dust. It’s also relatively quiet when it returns to the dock, and its anti-tangle brush and 8,200Pa of suction perform well on most carpets.

articles.title: Many of our favorite Blu-ray movies are over 50 percent off for Black Friday
articles.body:
No shade to those who love their subscription services, but viewing physical movies is a time-honored tradition that shouldn’t go away. Watching them doesn’t feel all that different, but deciding which movie to watch feels less annoying; sifting through a movie collection on your shelf or in a storage binder is so much more fun (and less overwhelming) than scrolling endlessly in apps.
Many of our favorite Blu-ray movies are over 50 percent off for Black Friday
Deck the shelves with discounted films, box sets, animated series, and more at some of the lowest prices we’ve seen.
While standard Blu-ray players that display movies at up to 1080p are fairly inexpensive, 4K Blu-ray counterparts that can show movies in all their 4K HDR glory are significantly pricier (but totally worth it if you’re a movie buff). No matter the player you own, there are always Blu-ray deals, and the discounts are especially good during Black Friday. We’ve highlighted some of our favorites below, though Amazon, Barnes & Noble, and Gruv are each overflowing with more deals than we could realistically wedge into our coverage.
KPop Demon Hunters
The once-Netflix-exclusive animated film is now available on 4K Blu-ray at a great price.
High and Low
Akira Kurosawa’s High and Low showcases how capitalism can rot our moral compasses.
Sinners
Ryan Coogler’s Sinners delivers a memorable plot with some fantastic mid-movie dance choreography. This movie’s part of Gruv’s “3 for $33” sale.
Star Trek: The Next Generation
Own the complete run of The Next Generation across 41 discs in 1080p resolution, currently the most hi-res option available.
The Lord of the Rings Trilogy
One of the best Black Friday deals, bar none. The set includes the theatrical cuts of the trilogy, plus the extended editions.
The Matrix: 4-Film Déjà Vu Collection
Setting aside that not every Matrix movie is amazing, the Déjà Vu set includes them all for less than if you bought them separately.
The Princess Bride
One of Rob Reiner’s many classics, but the only one with a truly fantastic, feisty line read from Mandy Patinkin.
The Before Trilogy
All three of Richard Linklater’s Before movies in one set, a remarkable achievement that shows the evolution of a romantic relationship over decades.
Interstellar
Christopher Nolan’s time-jumping adventure is a must-watch that’s still enjoyable after multiple viewings.
Seven Samurai
The 1956 samurai tale is all about banding together to become something bigger. This set includes the recent 4K restoration.
John Singleton’s Hood Trilogy
A 4K collection that includes director John Singleton’s acclaimed films Boyz n the Hood, Poetic Justice, and Baby Boy.
Neon Genesis Evangelion
All 26 episodes of the influential mecha anime in one set, plus a bunch of extras, including feature films, music videos, cast auditions, and more.
Speed Racer
The Wachowski sisters followed up their work as directors on the Matrix trilogy to create this awesome live-action take on the classic manga.
The Super Mario Galaxy Movie
If you liked the first Super Mario Bros. Movie, there’s more family-friendly fun where that came from in its follow-up.
Blade Runner 2049
It couldn’t have been easy to follow Ridley Scott’s original Blade Runner, but director Denis Villeneuve knocked it out of the park.
Over the Garden Wall
The beloved animated series came to Blu-ray in early 2026, giving viewers a more hi-res option after having to settle for DVD for over a decade.

articles.title: Michael Giles, co-founder and drummer of King Crimson, dies aged 84
articles.body:
Michael Giles, the drummer who co-founded prog rockers King Crimson, has died aged 84.
The news was announced by King Crimson’s record label DGM, who said he died on Monday 23 November, but did not give a cause of death.
“Michael was instrumental in establishing King Crimson as one of the most innovative and influential bands in the history of progressive music,” the statement reads. “His extraordinary rhythmic imagination, musical sensitivity and highly inventive approach to drumming were fundamental to the band’s pioneering sound.”
That skill and dexterity made a huge impact on the prog artists who followed him, including Rush drummer Neil Peart, who called Giles “a very important influence on me”.
Born in Bournemouth in 1942, Giles and his brother Peter sowed the seeds for King Crimson by advertising in a local newspaper for a bandmate: guitarist Robert Fripp answered it, and the trio formed Giles, Giles & Fripp, who alighted on an eccentric, sprightly jangle-pop style. They released their debut album The Cheerful Insanity of Giles, Giles & Fripp in 1968, which sold poorly and their label Deram rejected their next set of songs.
Ian McDonald joined the group, along with Fairport Convention singer Judy Dyble, though the group only recorded a handful of home-recorded songs before Peter Giles left later in 1968. Michael Giles, Fripp and McDonald forged ahead, forming King Crimson with Greg Lake and Peter Sinfield, debuting live in April 1969 and supporting the Rolling Stones in Hyde Park that summer.
Their debut album In the Court of the Crimson King, released in October 1969, was a sensation: a vision of rock music as not only heavy but shapeshifting, symphonic and mystical, it was an instant critical and commercial success, reaching the UK Top 5 and US Top 30. Giles’s deft drumming was a key ingredient, from the heavy tumbling fills of 21st Century Schizoid Man to lighter jazz-adjacent playing and pattering ghost notes, all with a sure-footed rhythmic sense that guided songs through shifts in time signature. “I was always interested in space, restraint and atmosphere, in allowing music to breathe rather than constantly filling it,” Giles later said.
Giles (as well as McDonald) then walked away from King Crimson, later citing a desire to “explore and develop new ideas for a much more expansive approach to playing drums and percussion into being equal and integral to my own compositions,” though he played as a session musician on King Crimson’s second album In the Wake of Poseidon, which returned them to the UK Top 5.
Giles and McDonald formed a duo, releasing the album McDonald and Giles in 1970, but thereafter Giles worked chiefly as a session musician. He backed Leo Sayer on his 1975 album Another Year, including the UK No 2 hit single Moonlighting; recorded with other prog figures such as Soft Machine’s Kevin Ayers and former Genesis member Anthony Phillips; and in 1993, played with Bryan Ferry on his cover of soul classic Taxi, plus there were numerous stints with other musicians.
He also reconvened with another ex-King Crimson member, Greg Lake, for the latter’s 1981 self-titled solo debut album; with McDonald again for McDonald’s only solo album, 1999’s Drivers Eyes; and in 2002 formed a band with various King Crimson alumni, 21st Century Schizoid Band.
Giles also released two solo albums, 2001’s Progress and, earlier this year, Shadows/Solo, a compilation of material recorded over a number of years. “It probably does reveal a more private and continuous thread running through the different phases of my life as a musician,” he said of the latter album in an interview with It’s Psychedelic Baby magazine. “What has always been important to me is to remain honest and genuine in the creative process, to make music only when it feels natural and truthful to do so … I have always preferred to allow the music to pass through me like a conduit, in its own time.”
He is survived by his five children: Tina, Amanda, William, Rosie and Oliver.

articles.title: Police reportedly turn water cannons on protesters outside Meta offices in India
articles.body:
Police in the Indian state of Haryana turned water cannons on protesters from the opposition Congress party outside Meta’s offices, according to Reuters. The protests are just the latest from the party’s youth wing, which has accused Meta of bowing to pressure from Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and censoring Congress party accounts.
Police reportedly turn water cannons on protesters outside Meta offices in India
India’s opposition party continues to pressure Meta over accusations of censorship.
Last week, protesters allegedly breached Meta offices in Delhi, demanding the company reinstate party leaders’ accounts. While some were reinstated, a representative of the Congress party’s youth wing, Manu Jain, told Reuters that “thousands” more remain restricted, and the party has accused the Modi government of trying to stifle free speech.
Meta did not respond to a request for comment on the continuing protests and escalating police response.
The Congress party has now filed a suit against Meta and the government. According to Reuters, a court filing claims that the country’s recently implemented rules regarding the removal of “unlawful” content have become “an instrument for the suppression of lawful political expression.”

articles.title: Scrapheap America
articles.body:
A Patch Three Pack
$20
Pretty sure everyone should be wearing gloves here.
I was in bed with the flu as America fell apart. I drifted in and out of fever dreams and incessant coughing jags, emerging long enough to discover yet another piece of critical infrastructure had suddenly failed. First it was email, then it was airplanes, then banks, then I lost track somewhere in the haze as one day blurred into two and then into three. Emerging from the other side, my lungs wrecked, my head aching—damaged, like the song says, bad at best—I felt like maybe I'd fared better than the various systems we rely on to, you know, function.
This isn't a post-mortem on what happened when everything went down. That's been done better than I could by the folks at 404 Media, who summed it up as the "philosophy of firing the experts and YOLOing AI into everything while hoping shit doesn’t break is now the explicit strategy of our entire economy and our entire government." It's not working.
It isn't just computer systems, which have been hit by a one-two punch of years of mass layoffs followed by AI-exposed security vulnerabilities that could have really used those hundreds of thousands of extra hands on deck right about now. It's pretty much every overwhelmed governmental entity, limping along since DOGE blew through last year like a tornado. It's your bank account, which if it's like mine, has entirely given up. It's gas prices. It's plane tickets. It's the cost of bread and shoes and every other goddamn thing.
As my pal Bree Bridges put it in the midst of the waterfall of breakdowns last week: "Everything costs too much and nothing works. You go broke paying for insurance that you can't even access until you pay even more money and after that they will try to prevent you from getting benefits in any way they can. food is poison, measles are back, cheeseburgers are luxury."
Things have been breaking for a long time now. The thing about having our country run by incompetents, grifters, and sycophants is that "broken" was always going to be the end state, it was just a question of how long it might take. Well, now we know: it's now. The whole country is peeling up like the Reflecting Pool liner.
When I'm as sick as I was in the last week (seriously, get your flu shot), there's one show that my body can handle: The late 1990s British engineering competition Scrapheap Challenge. I'm not sure why my body, when it's struggling to survive, wants to watch teams of working-class Brits run through a junkyard using a plasma cutter to separate an axle from an old London taxi, pull the motor from an old washing machine, or salvage a junked airplane and then make it fly, but Scrapheap has accompanied pretty much every major illness I've had for the last quarter century.
The premise of Scrapheap Challenge is simple. Two teams of three compete to build, over 10 hours, fully working machines capable of meeting whatever challenge has been laid out. That's meant teams building working trebuchets large enough to fling a car, firetrucks that can put out a blaze, demolition machines that can tear down walls, and every possible vehicle you can imagine and some you can not. All of it built from junked cars and rusted beams and every piece of scrap that's ever been tossed out. It's wildly inventive, often quite funny, and 100% a show that could not be made today because it's amazing that nobody ever cut off a body part or set themselves on fire.
At this point, I've seen every Challenge that's been lovingly preserved on YouTube, and so this past week I've drifted in and out of consciousness, half watching, half listening, and half discovering that, sandwiched between the teams "bodging" some contraption together, another system had collapsed in America.
The thing about everything breaking is that we have no real choice but to fix it. That's the challenge we all face right now in America, as things fall apart and there's nobody left to put it back together but us. But there's nothing saying that it has to resemble what came before. In Scrapheap Challenge parts are parts: raw materials to be reassembled into something that might work, given enough duct tape and crossed fingers. That's everything now: a vast field of scrap ready to be rebuilt into whatever we might need. The opportunity for imagination, for envisioning a life that's better than the one we've seen collapse around us, for building new and better and different is upon us. America is a scrapheap now, and it's up to us to rise to the challenge.
Published November 20, 2026. |
There's more where this came from. I write about fighting back, trying even when it's hard, and the things that keep me going. No cost, no spam, just me.
Or you can always subscribe via RSS or follow me on Mastodon or Bluesky where new writing is always posted.

I'm not sure why my body, when it's struggling to survive, wants to watch teams of working-class Brits run through a junkyard using a plasma cutter to separate an axle from an old London taxi, pull the motor from an old washing machine, or salvage a junked airplane and then make it fly, but Scrapheap has accompanied pretty much every major illness I've had for the last quarter century.
The premise of Scrapheap Challenge is simple. Two teams of three compete to build, over 10 hours, fully working machines capable of meeting whatever challenge has been laid out. That's meant teams building working trebuchets large enough to fling a car, firetrucks that can put out a blaze, demolition machines that can tear down walls, and every possible vehicle you can imagine and some you can not. All of it built from junked cars and rusted beams and every piece of scrap that's ever been tossed out. It's wildly inventive, often quite funny, and 100% a show that could not be made today because it's amazing that nobody ever cut off a body part or set themselves on fire.
At this point, I've seen every Challenge that's been lovingly preserved on YouTube, and so this past week I've drifted in and out of consciousness, half watching, half listening, and half discovering that, sandwiched between the teams "bodging" some contraption together, another system had collapsed in America.
The thing about everything breaking is that we have no real choice but to fix it. That's the challenge we all face right now in America, as things fall apart and there's nobody left to put it back together but us. But there's nothing saying that it has to resemble what came before. In Scrapheap Challenge parts are parts: raw materials to be reassembled into something that might work, given enough duct tape and crossed fingers. That's everything now: a vast field of scrap ready to be rebuilt into whatever we might need. The opportunity for imagination, for envisioning a life that's better than the one we've seen collapse around us, for building new and better and different is upon us. America is a scrapheap now, and it's up to us to rise to the challenge.
Published November 20, 2026. |
There's more where this came from. I write about fighting back, trying even when it's hard, and the things that keep me going. No cost, no spam, just me.

articles.title: Here’s what other Verge readers bought during Black Friday
articles.body:
We’ve covered a lot of deals so far that we think are fantastic during Black Friday, but readers gravitated to some more than others. Price plays a major factor, unsurprisingly, but for the holidays, some people care more about novelty above all else. They just want to gift something cool (or get something nice for themselves).
Here’s what other Verge readers bought during Black Friday
Cheap, practical gifts (and subscriptions) won over pricey ones during Black Friday.
Deals on streaming services were extremely popular with readers this year because the savings are outstanding, and I think most of us are sick of paying and arm and a leg for monthly access. You can save big on Disney Plus, Hulu, HBO Max, Peacock, and even Apple TV. Streaming aside, Verge readers proved they have good taste in gear as you can see below in our small collection of the most-bought products.
AirPods Pro 3
Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 deliver the best noise cancellation and sound quality of any AirPods yet, along with a more comfortable, secure fit and improved water resistance. They also feature built-in heart rate tracking for workouts and support live translations for a handful of languages. Read our review.
Disney Plus, Hulu Bundle
You can get an ad-supported Disney Plus and Hulu bundle for $4.99 a month ($8 off) for an entire year. Both streaming services feature a deep catalog of new and classic TV shows and movies, including The Simpsons, Andor, Toy Story 5, and The Fantastic Four: First Steps.
Anker Universal Charger (100W)
Anker’s durable travel adapter delivers up to 100W of power and works in over 200 countries. It doesn’t support AC plugs, but it does offer a trio of USB-C ports and a nifty LCD display to keep tabs on the charge percentage.
Xteink X4 Classic pocket e-reader
With a 4.3-inch E Ink screen, the Xteink X4 is smaller and more pocketable than any Kindle and Kobo model currently available. It has some drawbacks — it’s limited to TXT and EPUB files — but it’s great for tinkering; it also has a magnetic mount so you can stick it to the back of MagSafe-ready phones.
Govee Table Lamp 2
Govee’s Table Lamp 2 is way more fun than your average table lamp. The color-changing device boasts built-in scheduling and more than 60 dynamic lighting effects, including preset scenes for various holidays. You can even create custom color combos for when “Dandelion” and other presets just aren’t cutting it.
SwitchBot Bot Rechargeable
Do you ever wish you could turn on your coffee maker or hit the light switch without getting up? The SwitchBot Bot lets you do that. All you need to do is stick the inexpensive contraption on a standard button or rocker switch, which will allow you to control or schedule your pet feeder, garage door, and a wide range of other devices from your smartphone.
HBO Max
An HBO Max Basic subscription provides access to shows like A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, The Last of Us, and The Pitt, as well as films like Superman and Weapons. You can get a year of the monthly ad-supported subscription for $5.49 a month (about $6 off) until December 1st.
Wuben G5 rechargeable flashlight
The Wuben G5 flashlight is as small as a Zippo lighter, yet far more versatile, with a bright, rotatable light that can shine in numerous colors. It features USB-C charging and has an adjustable clip.
Kodak Charmera Keychain Digital Camera
The Chamera is not a good camera, but that’s not the point. Kodak’s charming, keychain-friendly tchotchke lets you snap lo-fi memories on a whim, with an ultra-small 1.6-megapixel sensor, a built-in LED flash, and the tiniest amount of storage. Read our hands-on.
Fanttik X9 Pro Portable Tire Inflator
The Fanttik X9 Pro can inflate a car tire in under a minute, making routine maintenance fast and easy. There are four one-click presets for cars, motorcycles, bikes, and balls, along with a manual mode that reaches a maximum pressure of 150PSI.
Peacock
Peacock is a great way to catch up on a wealth of content from NBC’s various networks, whether you plan to rewatch The Office or catch up on all things Bravo. A Premium subscription also grants access to films from studios like Universal Pictures and DreamWorks, along with live sports and a host of Peacock Originals.
Apple AirTag (second-gen)
Apple’s latest AirTags feature an upgraded ultra-wideband chip for more precise location tracking, a noticeably louder speaker, and an expanded Bluetooth range. Read our review.

articles.title: Anker’s 100W universal travel charger is down to $60, its lowest price yet
articles.body:
During Black Friday, the Anker 100W Universal Charger is on sale for $59.99 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, a $20 discount from its list price. That’s a few dollars lower than the previous best, with both the dark gray and silver versions available from all three retailers. With four USB ports and support for over 200 countries, you can keep all of your devices charged wherever you end up.
Anker’s 100W universal travel charger is down to $60, its lowest price yet
The fast charger has four USB ports and fits outlets in more than 200 countries. It’s $20 off for Black Friday.
Anker Universal Charger (100W)
Anker’s durable travel adapter delivers up to 100W of power and works in over 200 countries. It doesn’t support AC plugs, but it does offer a trio of USB-C ports and a nifty LCD display to keep tabs on the charge percentage.
Anker’s travel charger supports outlets in over 200 countries, including Type A for the United States, Canada, Japan, and China; Type C for the European Union; and Type G for the UK and Singapore. It doesn’t support Type I, the outlet used in Australia, New Zealand, and Argentina. Also, there’s no AC adapter. It’s a USB-only affair. To that end, you can charge up to four devices at once, with three USB-C ports and one USB-A port, with two of the USB-C ports capable of delivering up to 100W when used individually. There’s even a tiny display on the unit that lets you check how much power is going to your devices at a glance.

articles.title: The best Black Friday deals on our favorite smart home gear
articles.body:
I’ve spent my post-turkey haze powering through reams of deals on smart home gadgets to find the best discounts on some of my favorite products.
The best Black Friday deals on our favorite smart home gear
From smart party speakers to even smarter mixers, I’ve rounded up some of my favorite connected home gadgets you can grab on sale this weekend.
Smart home is often one of the best categories to shop around Black Friday, as it’s traditionally when robot vacuums, video doorbells, smart locks, and thermostats see their lowest prices of the year. And this year does not disappoint! Roborock’s flagship Saros 20 is under $1,000 for the first time, and Ecobee’s excellent Smart Thermostat Premium has finally dropped under $200 (for Costco members and today only).
I also spotted some great first-time discounts on the latest Birdbuddy smart bird feeder I reviewed this summer, along with the new Alexa digital photo frame I’m currently reviewing. This time of year is also a good opportunity to grab a bargain on higher-priced items you may have been eyeing for a while, such as Skylight’s giant 27-inch digital wall calendar, GE Profile’s fun smart mixer, and Aqara’s new high-tech UWB smart door lock that unlocks as you approach.
Here are some of the best deals I’ve spotted so far. We’ll keep this list updated, so check back often!
Govee Table Lamp 2 Pro X Sound by JBL
This RGB smart lamp packs a JBL speaker inside to combine snazzy lighting effects and decent sound into one fun, portable package. Battery-powered and with support for Matter, this is a smart light with party speaker aspirations. It’s the perfect size to add a little punch to your next gathering or snazz up a college dorm room. Read our review.
LIFX Everyday Smart Light Bulbs (two-pack)
LIFX’s dimmable, color-changing bulbs offer Wi-Fi connectivity, simple setup, and Matter compatibility, so they work with any major smart home platform. The company is currently trialing a Thread beta that will bring the option to add Thread connectivity to all its Matter devices.
Amazon Alexa Photo Frame
A 10-inch anti-glare touchscreen that comes in a few design options, it’s a frame that features Alexa and doubles as a smart speaker. It works with Amazon Photos, which offers unlimited storage for Prime members.
Aqara Smart Lock U400
This innovative new smart lock uses the U1 ultra-wideband (UWB) chip in many iPhones and Apple Watches to automatically unlock your door as you approach. It also works with the new Aliro standard, making it compatible with Android phones for hands-free unlocking. Read our review.
Birdbuddy Nook
The Birdbuddy Nook is the company’s least expensive and smallest model, and it packs a lot of bang for your buck. Its 4K HDR camera delivers excellent image quality, and a 3.8-cup seed capacity means less frequent refills. An optional solar panel extends the already good battery life. Read our review.
Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 Flow
Roborock’s first roller-mop robot vacuum, the Curv 2 Flow, features flagship specs at a midrange price, including excellent mopping, a retractable mop cover, 20,000Pa suction, AI-powered obstacle avoidance, and a compact design. Read our review.
Philips Hue Festavia string lights
These smart lights have beautiful colors, a nice selection of festive scenes, and an easy-to-use app. They are super reliable when paired with a Hue Bridge and also work over Bluetooth. They come in three lengths, work with all the major smart home platforms, and are Matter-compatible. Read our review.
Skylight Calendar Max
A digital touchscreen display designed to help families manage calendars, to-do lists, meals, and chores. It connects to Wi-Fi and features a 27-inch screen that can display photos when not in use. Read our review.
Reolink Video Doorbell PoE camera
Power over Ethernet provides this 2K resolution video doorbell with rock-solid connectivity while reducing the number of wires you need. There’s no subscription required to view recorded video; it can record locally on a microSD card, Reolink Hub, or FTP server and connect to a platform like Home Assistant.
Aura Aspen
Even if your mom lives halfway around the world, the Aura Aspen can help her feel close. The 12-inch display looks more akin to a traditional photo frame than other models, in part due to an antiglare screen, slim bezels, and a 4:3 aspect ratio. It can also automatically showcase images via Google Photos, iCloud Photos, or a companion app, the latter of which even allows for text captions. Read our review.
Narwal Flow 2
The Narwal Flow 2 is an excellent robot vacuum for hardwood floors. A superb mop with a wide flat roller pad and a good vacuum, the Flow 2 also has top-notch navigation and obstacle detection. Its sleek base station is also less of an eyesore than most models. Read our review.
Lutron Diva Smart Dimmer Switch Kit
This kit is everything you need to get started with Lutron’s excellent smart lighting system and turn your existing wired lights into smart ones that you can control from anywhere. It replaces your standard wall switch and works with all the major smart home systems, making it easy to dim or adjust multiple lights from your wall switch, your phone, or with your voice.
Eve Energy Smart Plug (Matter)
This smart plug offers the most detailed energy monitoring of any we’ve tested. It supports Matter over Thread and is a good choice for Apple Home and SmartThings users, as it offers energy monitoring on those platforms.
GE Profile Smart Mixer
This smart mixer is great for the tech-forward baker. With a built-in digital scale and Auto Sense and Active Stir to take some of the busywork off your hands, it features a high-powered motor with a 7-quart bowl. It’s compatible with all front-mounted KitchenAid attachments. Read our review.
SwitchBot Smart Candle Warmer
SwitchBot’s Matter-compatible Smart Candle Warmer lets you set schedules to turn it on and off in the app or any connected smart home platform and have pleasant scents waft safely throughout your home on demand.
Ring Battery Doorbell 2K
At more than half off, Ring’s 2K battery-powered video doorbell is a great deal, offering 2K video and easy installation. However, its battery is built in, so you’ll need to remove the doorbell to charge it via USB-C.
Echo Dot Max
The Echo Dot Max features a flat design and a redesigned sound system, which delivers nearly three times the bass as its predecessor. It also offers improved conversation detection and better noise filtering, thanks to Amazon’s new AZ3 chip. Read our review.
Roborock Saros 20
This bot can climb high transitions between rooms and get over obstacles, meaning it’s less likely to get stuck than other bots. The Saros 20 is also really slim — just 3.13 inches tall, small enough to squeeze under most furniture — and it’s equipped with excellent obstacle avoidance, making it a great robot for cluttered households. Read our review.
Govee Uplighter Floor Lamp
This fun smart lamp can light up your ceiling or cast a warm white reading light over a chair, making it super versatile. It has three separate lighting zones that can display white or color-changing lights and offers a huge array of dynamic effects. It supports Matter, so it will work with all the major smart home platforms.
Ecobee Smart Thermostat Premium
The Ecobee Smart Thermostat Premium is an excellent option for adding smarts and some style to your HVAC system. As well as being a smart way to control your energy use, the thermostat can also act as a video intercom for Ecobee’s excellent doorbell camera and an indoor air quality monitor. Read our review.

articles.title: The AI-designed USB-C LTE Modem is built, and it makes calls
articles.body:
All posts
We built the LTE modem: it registers on 4G, texts and makes calls
The LTE modem Koppar designed from a one-page spec has been built and brought up. It registers on 4G, sends texts and makes calls, and AI agents on the RealPCB benchmark are graded against its layout.
In October we published a 4-layer USB-C LTE modem that Koppar designed from a one-page spec: a Quectel EC25-EUX, an RP2040 acting as a USB sound card for the call audio, a USB hub and a 3.8 V buck, on an 85 × 65 mm board. It reached the front page of Hacker News, and the questions there were fair ones: would it ever be built, and would it work if it were?
It has been built, and it works. The board came back from JLCPCB assembled. We soldered the modules on by hand, and board 2 now works end to end: plugged into a Mac, it registers on the network, sends and receives texts, and places and answers calls with the audio on the computer’s microphone and speakers.
What we tested
The board first, without the module, on 10 and 11 November:
Then with the EC25-EUX fitted and a nano-SIM in, up to 22 November:
To use it every day we wrote Koppar Phone, a menu-bar app for macOS: texts, calls on the computer’s microphone and speakers, voicemail for the calls you miss, and the network in detail. It is in the repository with the firmware and a command line for macOS and Linux.
What went wrong
- The module, soldered by hand. Both boards needed a second soldering pass on the EC25. Board 1’s module now starts but doesn’t show up on USB: its USB pins (69 to 71) need reflowing. Next time the assembler places the module, or we ship a stencil for a hot plate.
- No recovery pads. The design review added pads for the RP2040’s bootloader, SWD and the module’s USB_BOOT, but the boards of this order were made from an export taken before they were added. To force the RP2040’s bootloader we bridged two pins of the flash chip with tweezers while plugging in.
- A warm reset behind the hub. The RP2040 sometimes failed to come back on USB after a warm reset, a known erratum of the chip. The firmware now updates itself over USB and works around it: 22 updates in a row, each back on its own in 5 to 20 s.
- A library bug. The USB stack that ships with the Pico SDK froze the board the second time the computer opened an audio stream. A newer version fixed it.
- Pulling the cable. Rev B cuts the module’s power the moment USB goes away, possibly in the middle of a write to its flash. The software now switches the module off cleanly before you unplug, and before the Mac shuts down. The board itself should hold its power up for a few seconds.
What Koppar did, and what a person did
Koppar designed the board from the spec: the schematic, the parts, the placement and the routing. It passed every check Koppar runs before release. A review against the datasheets then found 12 problems those checks don’t look for, from 35 Ω antenna feeds to a SIM socket facing into the board. Every one was fixed before ordering, and the copper was redrawn by hand. That is the board that works. The design review post has the list, and what we changed in Koppar because of it.
Bring-up adds to that list. Rev C wants real BOOT and RESET buttons, test pads at the module’s control pins, a “module on” LED, a way to sense the cable being pulled, and signed firmware updates. Today Koppar adds test points and recovery pads only when the spec asks for them, so this spec should have asked. The full list is in REV-C.md.
The reference in an AI benchmark
Esuna Labs picked this board for RealPCB, their benchmark of AI agents
laying out real production circuit boards. It is one of the 20 open-hardware example boards in
their repository (task pcb-6b4cc11f313f), and one of four they ran every
model on and show on the benchmark’s page.
Each agent gets the board with its 115 free parts unplaced and nothing routed, and two hours alone in KiCad. Its layout passes only if it is rule-clean and, on every quality measure the grader takes (decoupling loops, the buck’s switch node, ground under the signals, the crystals), no worse than the layout the board’s engineer released by more than a margin. On this board, that released layout is ours: rev B, the one on the desk above. The grader’s reference figures are its 271 vias and its 4.1 mm from the buck to its inductor.
Six frontier models ran it, each at its highest reasoning effort in its lab’s own agent:
Five of the six could not lay it out as well as the board we shipped, including both models at the top of the benchmark’s leaderboard. And they started from the parts and their connections. Koppar started from a one-page spec.
Build one
The design is open hardware (CERN-OHL-P-2.0). The repository has the KiCad project, the Gerbers, the JLCPCB assembly files, the firmware, the host software and the build notes: Koppar-AI/koppar-lte-modem. The EC25 is not on JLCPCB’s assembly line: deselect it when you order, then solder it yourself or send one for the assembler to place. Power it from a USB-C port that gives 3 A.
Sources
- The test results: README and REVIEW.md, “Bring-up results”
- What to change next: REV-C.md
- The October thread: Hacker News
- The benchmark: RealPCB, Esuna Labs (the runs on this board, in the
board picker under the page’s replay) and esunalabs/realpcb
(tasks/pcb-6b4cc11f313f: the task, the grader and its reference figures)
Describe the circuit. Get the board.
See what Koppar does

articles.title: Source Control from Hell
articles.body:
My first office job was at an enterprise that built software for a big telecom: a massive Delphi help desk application on Windows.
Let me tell you about how we managed source control process at the time.
First, you download the code from a shared folder (hosted on a trusted Windows server in a locked room). Build your thing, run the app, test it locally. Then you upload your changes to the shared folder and create a new ticket in the internal task tracker (also a Windows app). The ticket should have a list of the changes you’ve made, in a rich text editor, in a manual format somewhat resembling a patch. But it wasn’t a patch; it couldn’t simply be applied with a tool. Instead, the tech lead looks at the shared folder and your task and copies the relevant changes to his own integration folder. This usually took him a full day because the shared folder had a lot of changes, not all of them were ready to be integrated. Needless to say, if you simply pull a snapshot of the code from the shared folder, it would most likely fail to compile.
The most common problem was two people overwriting each other’s work. So if you wanted to upload your stuff to the shared folder, you had to stand up and announce in a loud voice that you were using the shared folder. No chat apps back in the day.
Imagine starting your career with this development experience! I did my best to improve it. At the time, almost everyone used FAR Manager, so I built a plugin that locked the folder when someone was using it, so others would get a warning. It became very popular because nobody really liked the old yelling system.
Then in 2009 I found git. It was still early days, way before GitHub went mainstream, but my tiny little brain was blown away. Holy shit, it maintains old versions. And you can work locally. And you can sync and exchange deltas. And it was insanely fast (compared to the very aptly named TortoiseSVN I’d experimented with earlier). I must have rewatched Linus’ talk a billion times. I created git repos for every project I had, preached it to my friends, and even gave my first tech talk about git at my university.
Sadly, my diplomatic skills were extremely rudimentary, and I couldn’t convince our tech lead to adopt git. He mumbled something about business value and how this new git thing lacked one. I left the company after two years but kept meeting up with old colleagues for beer. They were still using the shared folder process many years later. It was crude, it was hellish, and it worked for them just fine.

articles.title: This purple electric Chinese minivan can go up to 559 miles on a charge
articles.body:
Electric minivans could be the ultimate in utility, with room for passengers, gear, and huge batteries. While VW’s ID Buzz only gave us 200 miles of real-world driving on a charge in 2023, China’s BYD has just announced a flagship purple peoplemover that can go an estimated 559 miles (900 km) on electricity.
This purple electric Chinese minivan can go up to 559 miles on a charge
The BYD Whale should cost around $45,000, not that you’d be able to buy one here.
It’s called the BYD Whale, and some back-of-the-napkin math suggests it lives up to the name. The van would be bigger than a Honda Odyssey, bigger than a Chrysler Pacifica, and bigger than a Toyota Sienna, at 17.3 feet (5,270mm) long, 6.5 feet (1,996mm) wide, 6 feet (1,815mm) tall, and with a 123-inch (3,130mm) wheelbase.
According to an auto-translated press release, the vehicle should have room for seven passengers and seven suitcases at a time, not that the company has shown off its interior yet. You can see a prominent sensor cluster on its forehead, though, and it’ll come equipped with LiDAR for advanced hands-free driving.
CarNewsChina points out it’s actually not the first with 900 km of CLTC battery range on board — Geely’s all electric Zeekr 009 minivan also claims to offer up to 900 km of range in one configuration. But BYD’s also claiming the can charge its battery from 10 percent to 97 percent in just nine minutes, and it get you from 10 percent to 70 percent in five minutes, according to Electrek.
The Whale will also come in a 248-mile (400 km) plug-in hybrid version as well, and the company’s planning to ship it in China in Q1 of 2027 for around 300,000 yuan. That’s roughly $45,000. As we’ve reported, Chinese cars are becoming quite competitive. Will they make it to the US?

articles.title: The M5 MacBook Air just got its biggest discount since Apple raised the price
articles.body:
If you’ve been holding off on buying a new MacBook Air since Apple raised prices by $200 in June, you’re in luck. The 13-inch M5 MacBook Air is on sale at Amazon and Best Buy with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage starting at $999 ($300 off) for Black Friday, which is the lowest price we’ve seen since the hike. If you want a larger display, Amazon and Best Buy are also taking $300 off the otherwise identical 15-inch model with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage, dropping it to $1,199.
The M5 MacBook Air just got its biggest discount since Apple raised the price
The new promo drops Apple’s 13-incher to within $100 of its all-time low, easing the sting of recent price hikes.
The M5-equipped MacBook Air is a good middle ground if you need more power than the MacBook Neo — which, thanks to a $100 discount, is $599 — but don’t want to splurge on a MacBook Pro. Its faster chip, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage make it better suited for multitasking and creative work in apps like Photoshop and Premiere. You also get a higher-resolution display, better speakers, a backlit keyboard that makes typing in the dark easier, and faster ports. Plus, its sharper webcam supports Apple’s Center Stage feature, which automatically adjusts the framing to keep you in view during video calls.
Of course, the Air can’t match the performance or higher-end displays you can get with a MacBook Pro, whether you opt for an M5 model, the newer M5 Pro model with a PROLED XDR Display, or one of the M6-powered machines. A Pro may be worth the extra money if you regularly edit video or work on more demanding creative projects. But if you mostly need a laptop for work, browsing, and occasional photo or video editing, the M5 Air is more than capable.

articles.title: The new iPad Mini is getting its first major discount for Black Friday
articles.body:
We were big fans of Apple’s new iPad Mini when we reviewed it in early November, but its steep starting price of $699 was hard to swallow. Thankfully, the small tablet is already getting a sizable discount for Black Friday. Right now, Amazon and Walmart are both selling the 2026 iPad Mini with Wi-Fi and 128GB of storage starting at $599 ($100 off), its lowest price to date.
The new iPad Mini is getting its first major discount for Black Friday
Apple’s most portable tablet offers a larger OLED screen and water resistance.
The new Mini is a notable upgrade over its predecessor, with a larger 8.5-inch OLED display that delivers deeper blacks and better contrast than the previous model’s 8.3-inch LCD. Despite the bigger screen, the tablet itself is smaller and lighter, making it easier to carry. Apple also added IP67 dust and water resistance, so you have less reason to worry about where you use it. As my colleague David Pierce noted in his review, that made a big difference in his day-to-day use; he felt more comfortable handing the Mini to his spill-prone toddler or keeping it nearby in the kitchen to follow recipes. He even took it into the shower to keep watching a football game.
The upgraded A20 Pro chip also made apps load faster and demanding games run better in Pierce’s testing, while battery life held steady at around nine hours of screentime. At $599, though, the new Mini is still relatively expensive if you mainly want a tablet for browsing the web or streaming shows. The last-gen iPad Mini, which runs on Apple’s A17 Pro chip, is available for under $500 if you’d rather save another $100 and can live without the OLED screen and water resistance. But if you’ve been waiting for a more worthwhile upgrade to Apple’s smallest tablet, the current Black Friday discount makes the new model easier to justify.

articles.title: Apple’s latest AirTags have dropped to just $18 a pop for Black Friday
articles.body:
If you’re tired of constantly scrounging around for your lost belongings, Apple’s second-gen AirTags are on sale for an all-time low of $18 at Amazon, Walmart, and Best Buy. The handy location trackers have a list price of $29 each, but have been consistently available for around $24 since Amazon Prime Day in late June.
Apple’s latest AirTags have dropped to just $18 a pop for Black Friday
With a longer range, more precise tracking, and a louder chime, the new(er) AirTag could save you from a big headache.
The upgraded ultra-wideband chip and improved Bluetooth in the latest AirTag should provide more precise location tracking, with a range 1.5x wider than the first-gen model. The internal speaker is also 50 percent louder than the original, making it easier to find whatever item your AirTag is attached to, whether it’s buried deep in your couch cushions or at the bottom of your bag. Even without those improvements, though, AirTags are still a great option for Apple users looking for their keys or luggage, with up to a year of battery life on a single coin cell battery and compatibility with both iPhones and newer Apple Watch models.

If our sub-$30 Black Friday roundup has you hungry for more great gadgets at low prices, you can currently grab the Nothing CMF Buds 2A in black starting at $17.89 on Amazon for Black Friday, which is about $11 less than the MSRP and the lowest price we’ve seen. The wireless earbuds are discounted in all three colors; however, the light gray and orange sets are slightly more expensive at $19.99 ($9 off).
Nothing’s ANC-equipped earbuds are on sale for less than $20 for Black Friday
You can grab the surprisingly feature-packed set of earbuds in one of three colors.
Nothing CMF Buds 2A

My colleague Brandon Widder keeps some in his backpack as a backup pair of earbuds, and their IP54 water and dust resistance rating makes a great choice for light exercise and yard work.

articles.title: Google will soon share Android developers' addresses publicly
articles.body:
Google will soon share Android developers' addresses publicly
Their phone numbers and addresses will be published globally, starting on March 1, 2027.
Starting on March 1, 2027, Google will display Android developers' phone numbers and addresses with their apps, and users everywhere will be able to see them. As The Elec has reported, this decision has been met with criticism, specifically from smaller developers who operate out of their homes. Some of them have been opting to rent offices just so they won't have to declare their real address. "Disclosing developers' home addresses amounts to an invasion of privacy," one independent developer told the publication.
Google, like Apple, now requires developers to declare whether they're a trader under UK laws and the European Union's Digital Services Act (DSA). The company says they have to classify themselves as a trader if they intend to earn money from their apps in any way on a regular basis, and if they already have a consistent frequency of transactions. Developers will have to make their declaration by February 1, 2027. Once they classify themselves as a trader, they'll have to submit their business identity, phone number and address, which Google will display to users everywhere. Users in the UK and the European Economic Area will also see their business details and self-certification.
If they fail to comply with these requirements, Google could block their updates from rolling out. Ultimately, the company could remove their apps from the Play store, not just in Europe, but in all regions around the world. The Verge notes that Google doesn't accept PO Boxes for an address like Apple does, forcing people to think of ways to protect their identifying information while still earning money from their apps. Apple also won't be displaying developers' phone numbers and addresses globally like Google intends to do, only in the European countries covered by the laws requiring them.
A Google spokesperson told Engadget: "We take privacy seriously and are committed to protecting developer and user data. At the same time, we comply with applicable laws and recognize how important it is for users to have accessible support for the apps they install. Based on what we have heard from the developer community, we are exploring ways to minimize the developer information displayed publicly while making sure users can still easily reach developers for support."
Update 11/27/26 8:45PM ET: We updated this post with Google's statement.

articles.title: Show HN: Luciole Mono – terminal font designed for legibility
articles.body:
Type your own text. 11 pt (15 px) is a particularly crisp size.
Characters that must not be confused
- I l 1 |
- 0 O o
- ' ` "
- ; : , .
The zero is slashed and narrower than the O; i, j, l and r are redrawn with serifs to fill their cell.
Download
- LucioleMono-Regular.ttf 137 KB
- LucioleMono-Bold.ttf 141 KB
- LucioleMono-Italic.ttf 142 KB
- LucioleMono-BoldItalic.ttf 146 KB
Install
- Download the four files above.
- On Linux, copy them to ~/.local/share/fonts/ and run fc-cache -f. On macOS or Windows, open each file and choose “Install”.
- Choose “Luciole Mono” in your terminal or editor settings, then restart it.
About
Luciole was designed for visually impaired readers by Laurent Bourcellier and Jonathan Perez, at the Centre Technique Régional pour la Déficience Visuelle (typographies.fr). Luciole Mono keeps its design and fits it to a 620-unit grid: wide letters are compressed then thickened back, narrow letters are redrawn, and the bold is a lighter semi-bold so that counters stay open.
Luciole Mono is a derivative of Luciole. It is an independent project, neither made nor endorsed by the authors of Luciole. Known limitations and the full list of changes are in the README.

as foreshadowed a while ago, my journey has now come to an end. Unfortunately, this includes my work on Heretic, which has meant so much to me. I sincerely regret the inconvenience this will cause the community.
I am archiving this repository to preserve it in its current, high-quality state, and to prevent issue and pull request spam from turning it into a trash pile. I encourage interested contributors to organize on Discord, Matrix, or elsewhere, and decide whether and how to continue the project without me. I am deliberately not naming a successor, nor am I suggesting any particular infrastructure. The future of Heretic is now in the hands of all of you.
As AI continues to spread through your lives, you will find that controlling the models you use gradually transforms from an issue of Free Speech into an issue of Free Thought. AI will be the lens through which you see the world, not just a tool for getting things done. The fight for the ability to shape that lens yourself is nothing less than the fight for the humanity in you.
Farewell, my friends. In times like these, one should be proud to be labeled a heretic.

articles.title: Knuth: Moratorium on Error Reports
articles.body:
For more than fifty years I've been welcoming reports from readers of errors in my books, so that I can correct them before new copies are printed.
Alas, the rise of LLMs has increased the productivity of my readers so greatly that error reports are now being submitted much faster than I can read them!
This content is very important to me, and I wish to take personal responsibility for getting everything right. Therefore I insist on verifying everything carefully.
That takes time. But the amount of available time is now less than zero.
Random sampling indicates that the vast majority of errors that have been reported in recent weeks are repeats of issues already submitted by others.
Therefore, I shall not be able to look at any error reports submitted after 25 November, 2026, until I've posted an updated list of the known errors in whatever book is involved.
Please consult the list below to see if error reports are currently being accepted.
I apologize for having made errors in the first place, and for having limited ability to cope with more than one thing at a time. I shall do my best to get through the existing reports as soon as humanly possible.
Thanks in advance for your patience and understanding.
